title: Kodak Launches Unique AirTag Rival With E-Ink Display
content:
Kodak licensee Reto this week introduced the SlideTag, a $34.99 Find My-compatible item tracker with a color E Ink screen for displaying personal photos.


The SlideTag's design draws on Kodak's Kodachrome slide mounts, placing a square display inside a retro frame with an attachment point for a keyring. Its 1.54-inch screen has a resolution of 240 × 240 pixels and uses six ink colors to reproduce images. As it is an E Ink panel, it retains a static image without needing continuous power to display it.

Users can manage photos through the Kodak Memory Link app for iOS and Android, separately from the accessory's tracking features. They can transfer up to 12 images over Bluetooth and arrange them into slideshows, or use the screen to display information such as contact details, a QR code, or a to-do list.

Find My app, the SlideTag can be located through the ‌Find My‌ network. There is also support for Google's Find Hub. A built-in buzzer provides an audible way to find nearby belongings.

AirTag, but slightly thinner. Apple's tracker measures 31.9mm in diameter and 8mm thick, and weighs 11.8 grams.

The ‌AirTag‌ retains some advantages, including Ultra Wideband technology for Precision Finding, which provides distance and directional guidance to nearby items on compatible devices. The ‌AirTag‌ also has a higher IP67 rating, providing protection against immersion in water up to one meter deep for up to 30 minutes.

Reto, which also makes the Kodak-branded Charmera keychain camera, is selling the SlideTag as a collectible. Buyers receive a randomly selected design in sealed packaging, rather than choosing a particular finish. There are eight standard designs and a secret edition that has a one-in-64 chance of appearing.

available to order from Reto's online store for $34.99.

title: Apple Still Working on Giant Foldable iPad That Could Cost $5,000
content:
Apple is still developing a large foldable iPad despite ongoing technical challenges and uncertainty about whether it will ever launch, according to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman.


Speaking on the latest episode of the "Power On" podcast, Gurman revived discussion about the device, known internally as "Project J312." He described it as a foldable iPad with a display measuring around 19 to 20 inches, saying it would resemble a "gigantic iPhone Duo with no display on the outside." The device could cost between $3,000 and $5,000.

Apple apparently originally wanted to announce the device by 2027, before pushing that target to 2028. The timeframe has since slipped to around 2029, although Gurman cautioned that it remains uncertain whether the product will ever reach the market.

Gurman cited cost and display manufacturing yield issues among the obstacles facing development, along with concerns that the ‌iPad‌ could be cumbersome. Apple has also yet to determine which operating system it would run, with macOS, iPadOS, and an entirely new platform all remaining possibilities. Gurman described the unresolved software direction as another complication, but expressed excitement about the device's potential.

report from research firm Omdia in September, which claimed that Apple had canceled plans for a foldable MacBook measuring between 16.1 and 18 inches when unfolded. Earlier reports had described that device as a large-screened foldable ‌iPad‌, although it remains unclear whether Omdia was referring to the same project Gurman discussed.

discussed the foldable ‌iPad‌ in April, describing it as a priority for John Ternus while warning that it could remain an unreleased experiment. The potential 2029 timeframe was already part of Gurman's report from October 2025, when weight and display technology issues were said to threaten Apple's earlier 2028 target.

title: Apple Faces Korean Regulator Review Over iPhone 16 AI Advertising
content:
Apple is facing a formal probe in South Korea over allegations that its iPhone 16 advertising misled consumers about the availability of Apple Intelligence features.


Investigators at the country's Fair Trade Commission (FTC) have referred Apple and Apple Korea for review, alleging that several Apple Intelligence features were not delivered as advertised, including Genmoji, Image Playground, and Siri's ability to understand personal context and onscreen awareness.

The allegations focus on whether Apple adequately explained which features were available and when others would arrive. For example, the FTC's report notes that Siri's personal-context capabilities were advertised for Korean availability in early April 2025 but did not arrive until October 2026, approximately 18 months later.

Apple provided MacRumors with the following statement:
"At Apple, we deeply value the relationship with our customers in Korea and have always focused on delivering the best products and services in the world. Since we added Korean language support for Apple Intelligence last year, users have benefited from dozens of powerful features that are integrated across Apple's platforms. And we have continued to build on that commitment with the recent launch of Korean language support for Siri AI, an entirely new version of Siri that's more capable, conversational, and personal. We have cooperated with the KFTC's investigation and disagree with the conclusions in the Examiner's Report. We look forward to presenting a fulsome defense before the Commission."
The Commission has yet to issue a final ruling or impose a penalty.

removed its "available now" marketing claim on its Apple Intelligence page, following a National Advertising Division inquiry. The advertising watchdog found that the wording implied that all listed features were available, and that a footnote explaining the phased rollout was insufficiently clear. Apple disagreed with the findings but ultimately complied with the recommendation.

$250 million settlement in May 2026 over a U.S. class-action lawsuit alleging it misled buyers about the availability of Apple Intelligence and Siri features when the iPhone 16 was released in September 2024.

title: How to keep watching DVDs with VLC as Apple phases out Mac DVD support
content:
Apple has started retiring the technology behind its built-in DVD playback starting in macOS 27. Here's how you can still watch discs on a Mac with an optical drive and VLC.

VLC on Mac
For now, the change affects developers, not people watching DVDs on their Macs. Apple has removed the DVDPlayback framework from the macOS 27 SDK, so developers can no longer build apps against it with that SDK.
The framework itself remains in macOS 27, and Apple says it won't be removed until a future release. DVD Player also remains available and functional in macOS 27.
If you have movies on DVD, you don't have to wait for another macOS update to find a different way to play them. The free VLC app can open a DVD as a disc, giving you access to its movie, menus, chapters, audio tracks, and subtitles.

title: 1Password Security Breach: What Was Accessed and What Wasn't
content:
Popular password management app 1Password today said it experienced a security breach earlier this month. 1Password says some customer names and email addresses were accessed, but no customer vault contents were compromised.


On November 19, 1Password saw indications that an employee's GitHub account had been breached and began investigating. The company says the breached GitHub account was used to access source code and push malicious code to backend services, with the code downloading some customer data. Here's a list of what the hacker was able to get:

 	
Names and email addresses customers use to sign into 1Password

 	
Account and user identifiers, and account creation and last sign-in times

 	
Public keys

 	
Secure Remote Password protocol parameters (1Password says this can't be used for account access)

 	
Tokens in emailed links for invitations, provisioning, and account recovery

 	
Other non-secret account data related to 1Password's internal architecture, like version numeric identifiers and file numeric identifiers

 	
1Password source code, which 1Password says does not include customer data or user secrets

 	
Access to 1Password's CI/CD system, which it says has infrastructure-related secrets for the service to work


According to 1Password, there is no impact to its services, availability, or product security. Customer vaults and the items in them were not accessed, nor were the keys that protect vaults. The hacker did not have access to account recovery keys or 1Password apps and browser extensions. 1Password vaults are encrypted and protected by keys on the user end, so content is not accessible to 1Password or anyone who hacks the 1Password servers.

The biggest risk comes from the token breach. Tokens can be used for account recovery, but they only work when paired with an SSO sign-in or a six-digit code sent to a user's email address. Codes have now been changed from six numeric digits to 10 alphanumeric characters to make them more difficult to brute force.

The affected GitHub account has been disabled, and the attacker's token was revoked. Internal credentials that may have been exposed have been revoked. Internal GitHub, CI/CD, and endpoint controls have been "tightened," with new detection methods for similar attacks. The company found no internal evidence of user account takeovers or compromise using the exposed account provisioning tokens, and it has hired independent cybersecurity experts to validate its response.

1Password users who had a token accessed were notified, but it is unclear if 1Password has sent notices about the breach to all users. While the blog post is titled as "update on" a security incident, it does not seem that the breach was disclosed when 1Password first learned of it six days ago.

1Password will not contact users to ask for an account password or Secret Key, and the information should be entered only in the official 1Password app or official website. It recommends all users be cautious about phishing attempts like emails, texts, and calls that mention 1Password or account recovery.

title: 1Password has been hacked–passwords are safe, but admin data was accessed
content:
Macworld





1Password is one of the most popular password managers, and one we’ve frequently recommended here at Macworld. Unfortunately, it has just suffered a major security incident.
On November 19, a malicious attacker gained access to a 1Password employee’s corporate GitHub account. They used that to access the 1Password source code and get access to the company’s backend services, which holds the administrative data for customers.
That’s stuff like customer names and email addresses, as well as public keys (but not private keys), account creation and sign-in times, and the like.
The good news for 1Password customers is that the content of user “vaults” were not compromised. That includes passwords and the other info that 1Password stores (like most password managers these days, 1Password can store payment info, addresses, and other data you may wish to auto-fill in forms). 1Password relies on private keys to decrypt passwords and other vault info, which are all hashed and salted so that even if an attacker decrypted one record it couldn’t get access to others.
1Password does not store your account password nor your secret key, which is used to generate the private keys stored on your own devices and necessary to access your encrypted info. All of that stuff is still safe. 
In the wake of the incident, 1Password disabled the GitHub account and revoked its key, rotated or revoked all internal credentials, lengthened the codes used in invitation and recovery emails from six digits to ten characters, and brought in an external cybersecurity firm to audit their efforts.
The company makes the following recommendations to users:
Be cautious about phishing attempts in the form of unexpected emails, texts or calls that mention 1Password, invitations, or account recovery attempts.
1Password will never contact you to ask for your account password or Secret Key. Only enter them in the official 1Password app, or on our official website, and only when you’ve opened the app or typed the address yourself. Your Secret Key is only needed the first time you sign in on a new device or browser.
Keep your Secret Key and account password safe.
If you see something suspicious, email support@1password.com.

title: An OLED MacBook Air is coming in 2028. Will it glow?
content:
Macworld





Last year, Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman reported that Apple has plans to update the MacBook Air with an OLED display in 2028. In his most recent Power On podcast, Gurman reiterated those plans, claiming that OLED will be part of a MacBook Air “overhaul” over the next 12 to 15 months.
The current MacBook Air design was introduced in 2022. While the design is soon-to-be five years old, it doesn’t feel dated and aligns with the other Pros without a touch display. But now that a new laptop design has been introduced with the PROLED XDR Display, Apple will quickly move to update its other laptop designs so they don’t lose momentum.
What would a MacBook Air “overhaul” look like? Even though the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display isn’t all that visually different from the mini-LED MacBook Pro that Apple still sells, it’s different enough to set it apart in the line. Besides the OLED display, it features thinner bezels and rounder corners that expand the usable space further toward the bottom of the display (and macOS does a really cool trick with those corners). It also has a Dynamic Island instead of a notch.
More importantly to the Air line, the PROLED laptop is slightly smaller and noticeably lighter. The 14-inch PROLED XDR MacBook Pro weighs 3 pounds, about a half-pound less than the non-touchscreen model and about a quarter-pound heavier than the 13-inch Air, which weighs 2.7 pounds. If Apple can get the 13-inch Air down to 2.25 pounds or so, it’ll make a dramatic difference.
The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display’s major new feature is a touchscreen tandem OLED, but I don’t expect the MacBook Air to get such a high-end screen. These are premium features that Apple will keep on its Pro laptop–a tandem OLED is a costly component to put into an Air. More likely is that the 2028 Air will not have a touchscreen, and it will have a single OLED panel similar to the one in the iPad mini.
So, a thinner, lighter, OLED MacBook Air with more usable screen space. Sounds pretty nice. But what about the glowing Apple logo? It would be cool to see it on the 2028 MacBook Air, but I’m not counting on it. I think Apple will keep it as a MacBook Pro feature to set it apart from the Air and MacBook Neo. But who knows, maybe Apple decided it’s part of the design language covering all its laptops. That would be a nice touch.

title: Apple has made an iPad that runs macOS, but we’ll probably never see it
content:
Macworld





The release of the touchscreen MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display has given new life to an old question in the Apple community: Will Apple ever release macOS on the iPad? We may finally have an answer, and it’s probably not one people are going to like.
On the latest edition of the Power On podcast, Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman said in no uncertain terms, “At this point, I don’t think that’s going to happen anytime soon.” Gurman revealed that Apple actually has iPads running macOS within Apple Park, but not for the purpose of releasing macOS on iPad to the general public. It’s for developing Mac-like features for iPadOS such as multitasking, and rebuilding Mac apps like Final Cut Pro for iPad. However, he cautions, “There is no work being done to consumerize macOS on the iPad,” said Gurman.
He’s on the side of the people who aren’t happy with that decision, however. “There are logic for the iPad. So they’re re-building a lot of the Mac and bring it to the iPad piece by piece, versus bringing the whole operating system to the iPad, he said. “In my view, I think they should just launch a 15-, 16-inch iPad and just bring Mac OS to it and just rip the Band-Aid off.”
But Guman notes that there’s another reason for keeping the iPad on iPadOS that’s complicates things further. In the European Union, it’s “better” for Apple to have distinct operating systems for its hardware segments, due to regulations. Considering how Apple swapped out Lightning on the iPhone due to EU regulations, it seems very unlikely that macOS will be released for the iPad.
Gurman does offer one glimmer of hope. Apple has been rumored to be working on a super-sized foldable iPad, something and opens up to a 19- or 20-inch display. Gurman said “it’s been facing a lot of issues” and was originally scheduled for 2027, but it’s been pushed out to 2029, if Apple decided to release it at all. Gurman said Apple is still undecided as to what operating system it will run. It could run macOS, iPadOS, or “something entirely new.”

Portable power banks that charge your phone are popular, but wireless battery packs using Apple’s magnetic MagSafe technology offer a simpler and smarter cable-free solution for iPhone 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18 and Air users. Special models that fit the iPhone Duo have also started appearing, and we’re testing them as they arrive at the Macworld Lab.
Phone batteries are prone to run dry just when you’re heading away from a power source, so having a portable charging source is one of today’s necessities. Annoyingly, most power banks require you to carry around a cable, too. Wireless power banks do away with cables but come with their own major limitation—the inefficiency of wireless charging means you need a high-capacity power bank to fully charge a drained iPhone.
MagSafe is a technology that’s compatible with all iPhone 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18, Air and Duo models, from the mini to the Pro Max, but strangely missing from the 16e model. It allows accessories to clamp magnetically to the back of the iPhone, making the charging connection more efficient. Most standard magnetic power banks will connect with the iPhone Duo but are too long to maintain a firm grip when handled or placed in a pocket or bag—look for power banks designed specially for that model..
We put the best portable chargers through a series of rigorous iPhone recharging tests, and have listed the winners by power, portability and functionality:
Best high-capacity 10k MagSafe power banks
Best small portable 5K magnetic power banks
Best multi-device charging MagSafe power banks 
Best power banks for iPhone Duo

You should consider size when it comes to a power bank: physical size and battery capacity. The higher the battery capacity, the more recharging power you’ll get from the power bank—but you’ll also be carrying around a larger, heavier item. Lighter, slimmer power banks are easier to pocket even when clamped to your phone. Larger power banks might not fit in your trouser pocket and can slide off easier when pocketed even if clamped magnetically.
10K power banks (with a 10000mAh battery capacity) can charge a phone close to two times over, while 5K (5000mAh) battery packs usually stretch between 60-75%, which is often enough to get you to the next wall-socket powering opportunity. If you are relying on the power bank for long-haul travel or a camping trip, a 10K battery or higher will suit you better. Belkin even offers a mid-range 8K power bank.
Milliamp hours (mAh) is quite a blunt measurement of battery capacity. It’s great for quickly differentiating between power bank sizes but we also list the capacity in the more accurate watt hours (Wh).
Also, look out for power banks that are built using the latest semi-solid-state battery technology that uses less liquid electrolyte than standard litium-ion power banks, making them more durable, longer lasting, and safer.
Wireless power bank charging speed
Wireless charging speeds vary from 7.5W (MagSafe Compatible) to 15W (certified MagSafe and Qi2), all the way to the very fastest wireless charging at 25W (Qi2.2). While it’s not as efficient as using a cable to charge a phone, magnetic wireless charging is a step closer to doing away with cables altogether. Qi2 25W brings wireless charging close to wired speed but only iPhones 16 and later support that speed, and some power banks include a built-in USB-C cable for even faster charging up to 45W. The iPhone Air can manage 20W max on even a 25W charger. See Which wireless tech is best for your iPhone?.
We have listed the speeds at which each portable power bank can be charged itself (Input charger) and charge the iPhone (Output charger). The higher the wattage, the faster the charging should be.

A 10000mAh (10K) battery is the sweet spot for both power and portability. 5000mAh (5K) power banks reviewed further down are slimmer, lighter and easier to pocket, but generally offer a maximum of 70-80% recharge potential versus a 10K power bank that should be able to recharge an iPhone at least one and a half times over.

How we tested
MagSafe charger testing was conducted using an iPhone 16, 17 or 18 Pro, subscribed to a 5G network and WiFi, with screen off and all default settings.
Our test is a simple battery recharge shootout. We let our test-unit iPhone Pro (3095mAh battery capacity) drain to just 10% and then set the Battery Pack to work recharging the phone. We then assigned the charger a score of whatever percentage it managed to charge the iPhone to and subtract the 10%; we test each model at least twice.
It’s not a real-world test of day-to-day use where you’ll likely be using your phone for various tasks (of varying battery usage) and in different environmental conditions and network configurations. But it does give us a common score format that we can use to compare different battery-pack models.

				
					

				
			
Why is magnetic wireless better?
The MagSafe connection to Apple’s iPhone is precise enough to make wireless charging more efficient as around 20% of non-magnetic power loss is from poor placement of a phone and the wireless charging pad. Standard Qi wireless charging can lose as much as 50% of the portable battery’s power, but MagSafe and Qi2 wireless charging loses ‘just’ 30%. Hot out of the gadget laboratory, the new Qi 2.2 (also known as Qi2 25W) brings even faster 25W wireless charging for the iPhone 16, 17 and 18. 15% will be plenty fast enough for most of us but who doesn’t want the fastest possible charging when your iPhone’s battery icon is in the red?
Why comparing Watt Hours is better than Milliamp Hours
Phone batteries are generally rated in Milliamp Hours (mAh) but this is a measure of electrical charge, while a Watt Hour is equal to one watt of energy consumed for one hour of time.
When comparing battery capacities and how much a power pack will boost a phone’s internal battery, energy is more important than electrical charge.
And mAh ignores a battery voltage, which determines the wattage (power) of a battery.
If the mAh is the same, the higher the voltage, the greater the actual stored power.
For example, Apple’s MagSafe Battery Pack is rated at just 1460mAh but it has a higher voltage potential (7.62V) than the iPhone (3.81V) or other battery packs, meaning that it can provide more power to an iPhone than its mAh suggests; in fact, it is actually 2920mAh.
To go into further depth about this read our feature iPhone battery capacities compared that also lists all iPhones battery life in mAh and Wh.
Anatomy of a magnetic power bank

				
					

				
			
TORRAS




A lot more than a battery goes into the making of a magnetic power bank.
Of course, the battery is the most important component, but the wireless charging coils and magnetic connection are vital for efficient and therefore fast and powerful charging. The transmitter coil transfers power by electromagnetic induction.
The magnets need to be set up to exactly connect the transmitting coils—here on the power bank— to the receiving coils, in this case inside the iPhone.
The example shown above is the Torras MagStall Wireless Power Bank, reviewed in our chart. You can see the various parts, including that power bank’s rotating stand/handle.
Which magnetic wireless tech is right for each iPhone?
iPhone 7 and earlier: Don’t support wireless charging. 
iPhone 8 – iPhone X/XS/XR: Support wireless charging. iPhone 8 and later can charge wirelessly at 7.5W but on a less efficient non-magnetic Qi pad.
iPhone 11 and earlier: Don’t support MagSafe. iPhone 8 and later can charge wirelessly but on a less efficient non-magnetic Qi pad.
iPhone 12 – iPhone 15: Support MagSafe and Qi2. Can wirelessly charge at 7.5W with “MagSafe-Compatible” power banks and chargers, and at 15W with certified MagSafe or Qi2 power banks and chargers.
iPhone 16 – iPhone 18, plus iPhone Duo: Support MagSafe, Qi2 and Qi2.2. Can wirelessly charge at 7.5W with “MagSafe-Compatible” power banks and chargers, at 15W with certified MagSafe or Qi2 power banks and chargers, and at 25W with Qi2.2-certified power banks and chargers.
Is charging via a cable faster or safer than magnetic wireless charging?
Charging via a cable is nearly always faster than wireless, even the latest Qi2.2 wireless chargers. Wireless charging is inefficient, losing some of its energy transfer through heat, for example. MagSafe, Qi2, and Qi2.2 magnetic connections dramatically improve efficiency but sticking a cable in is still a faster method, if not as convenient.
Most magnetic wireless power banks include at least one USB-C port, and some even include a port and an integrated cable for ultimate convenience. Models after the iPhone 17 can charge to 50% in 20 minutes or under via a cable and a 45W or higher charger or power bank. But wireless is so simple and cable-free that we don’t mind waiting an extra 15 minutes or so to reach such a charge wirelessly.
Why does my phone occasionally charge slowly or even stop charging?
This phone charging behavior is due to the built-in battery management feature on your iPhone. A phone heats up during charging as power is exchanged between the charger’s coils and the iPhone’s own. The phone actively adjust its charging behavior accordingly. This can slow down or temporarily pause charging to protect battery health and extend its lifespan. This is completely normal. Once the phone cools down, charging will automatically resume as normal.
What is a semi solid state battery?
The material that carries ions back and forth inside a battery is called “electrolyte”. Traditional lithium-ion batteries use a volatile, free-flowing liquid for electrolyte. As their name suggests, solid-state batteries use a solid material such as a ceramic or polymer. But semi-solid-state batteries are more common in today’s new generation of power banks.
A semi-solid-state battery uses a mix of solid particles in a much smaller amount of liquid, making a hybrid thick gel, paste or slurry. By reducing the liquid content to a minimum, semi-solid-state batteries increase stability and durability and significantly lower the risk of leaks, fires, and dangerous thermal runaway.
What about non-wireless power banks?
Wireless charging—especially magnetic wireless charging—is super convenient and does away with the need to carry around messy cables to connect your device to the battery pack.
But wired charging is nearly always faster and not much of an inconvenience if you are not out and about. Over on our sister site Tech Advisor I have reviewed the best power banks that includes standard non-wireless battery packs that might be a decent solution as well as the power banks reviewed above.
Do magnetic power banks work when the iPhone is in a case?
Yes, most quality iPhone cases are compatible with MagSafe having their own magnet ring to ensure a close connection between the power bank’s magnetic charging coils and the iPhone’s own. You can find exactly which are supported in our roundups of the best iPhone 18 cases, best iPhone 17 cases, and best iPhone 16 cases.
We round up a selection of battery cases for iPhone here: Best iPhone Battery Cases.

title: $799 Smart Glasses Promise Vision Pro-Style Controls in a 45g Frame
content:
Hong Kong startup Savage Technology has announced its first product, "Orrorin Glasses," promising Vision Pro-style pinch controls and full-color displays for both eyes in a frame weighing just 45 grams.


The company describes the glasses as offering "Vision Pro–level interaction" and being around 25 times lighter than Apple's headset, including its external battery. Savage highlights the bulky hardware currently required for Apple's spatial computing experience, although Orrorin offers substantially fewer capabilities.




Savage says small pinches performed at the user's side control the interface without a ring, wristband, or controller. Eye tracking makes the display fade when the wearer looks away, rather than selecting interface elements as it does on Vision Pro.

lacks positional tracking and spatial mapping, so it cannot anchor virtual windows in a room like Vision Pro. 

Orrorin is the first product from Savage Technology, co-founded by Bill Pei and Elena Shi, and remains in engineering validation for now. The company is currently targeting developers with third-party apps and interaction with AI agents such as Claude Code and Codex.

title: Apple Has an iPhone Notifications Problem
content:
Apple has rules in place that are supposed to protect iPhone users from unwanted advertising in push notifications and Live Activities, but some apps appear to be flouting these rules, and Apple does not appear to be consistently enforcing them.


Apple's App Store guidelines do allow iPhone apps to send push notifications for promotions or direct marketing purposes, but only if users have "explicitly opted in to receive them via consent language displayed" in the app, and so long as the app provides a method "for a user to opt out from receiving such messages."

Push Notifications should not be used for promotions or direct marketing purposes unless customers have explicitly opted in to receive them via consent language displayed in your app's UI, and you provide a method in your app for a user to opt out from receiving such messages.
Unfortunately, there are some examples of apps ignoring this guideline.

On my iPhone in Canada, there are several apps that send me push notifications containing promotions without offering a way to opt out of these promotion-specific notifications, such as Cineplex, McDonald's, and Wendy's.

Canadian food delivery app Skip does offer a setting to turn off promotional notifications, but it has continued to send them to me long after I opted out.


Do you have any iOS apps that don't respect your promo notification settings or don't let you turn off promo notifications as Apple requires?

Let me know for a MacRumors story!

— Joe Rossignol (@rsgnl) November 25, 2026



A few MacRumors readers informed us that after they turned off DoorDash notifications for offers specifically and then place a delivery order, the app will prompt users to re-enable notifications so they "never miss an order update," even though they still have notifications enabled for order updates. The wording of this prompt can trick users into thinking that they might not receive order updates, but tapping the button re-enables offers.

app design guidelines saying "don't use a Live Activity to display ads or promotions" under "best practices." Apple's App Store guidelines say apps should not send users "unsolicited messages" via Live Activities.


Never expected to see anything like this https://t.co/GbdRIfqaE2
— Out of Galaxy (@OutofGalaxyy) November 22, 2026



If you know of other offending apps, let us know in the comments section. There are more.

Apple recently sent out its own App Store notification advertising a Paramount+ subscription deal, but the App Store does offer an option to opt out. Open the App Store, tap on your profile picture in the top-right corner, tap on Notifications, and turn off Recommendations & Offers. However, it is not clear if Apple obtained explicit consent from users as its App Store guidelines require. Of course, the App Store is a preinstalled app, so it technically does not have to follow the rules that Apple sets for third-party App Store apps.


PUSH ads now?! https://t.co/WRBndvxbE3
— Dylan (@DylanMcD8) November 21, 2026



All in all, it appears that Apple needs to do more to crack down on apps that are violating its rules surrounding advertising in push notifications and Live Activities.

Black Friday is a great time to buy an iPad, with discounts spanning affordable everyday tablets, powerful Pro models, and clearance stock from previous generations. This year’s standout Black Friday iPad deal so far is on Apple’s newest tablet. Amazon has listed the 128GB iPad mini (A20 Pro) for $599 in the U.S., $100 off. 
For most people, we’d recommend the 11-inch M4 iPad Air. Amazon has listed the 128GB Wi-Fi model for $649 in the U.S. and £669 in the U.K., saving $100 and £80, respectively. If you mainly want an iPad for browsing, streaming, or schoolwork, the 128GB A16 iPad at $379 is the cheaper U.S. option. It’s $20 below its October Prime Day price, although it still costs $30 more than it did before Apple raised prices in June. 
The biggest savings are on configurations with more storage. Amazon has listed the 11-inch M5 iPad Pro with 1TB for $1,499 in the U.S. a saving of about $300. In the U.K. AO has the 1TB 11-inch iPad Pro for £300 off. Those are worth a look if you need the extra space. The standard A16 iPad and iPad mini are excluded. Apple is also offering a $25/£20 gift card with eligible purchases of the Apple Pencil Pro or a Magic Keyboard for the iPad Air or iPad Pro. The gift card is for a future purchase. See our full guide to Apple’s Black Friday offer.
Which iPad should you buy this Black Friday?


M4 iPad Air – Our best all-round choice

				
					

				
			
Apple Inc




The iPad Air offers a strong balance of performance, screen size, and price without the premium cost of the Pro. The 11-inch model suits buyers who prioritize portability, while the 13-inch version gives you more room for multitasking and creative work.
A good Black Friday discount could make either size an attractive purchase. Compare storage capacities carefully, though: a larger advertised saving on a high-capacity model isn’t necessarily better value if you don’t need the extra space. 
U.S. Black Friday price: At Amazon, you can already get a saving of $100 off some iPad Air models, although in some cases these are selling out, in which case we are seeing Best Buy match the $100 off.  
U.K. Black Friday price: Amazon has £80 to £109 off the iPad Air configurations. For example, you can get the 11-inch M4 iPad Air with 128GB for £669, down from the usual £749. These are reasonable savings, although we saw better discounts during October Prime Day, with up to £144 off. Last Black Friday, selected M3 Air configurations received £100 discounts.
Apple’s deal: You can get a $100/£80 Apple Gift Card when you buy an 11-inch or 13-inch M4 iPad Air from Apple, which is similar to the Amazon U.K. deal. 






iPad Pro – Best for demanding creative work

				
					

				
			
Apple Inc




The iPad Pro is the option for buyers who need Apple’s highest-end tablet performance and premium display. It comes in 11-inch and 13-inch sizes, but its capabilities – and price – will exceed what many people need for browsing, streaming, and everyday apps.
We’d look for a substantial saving rather than buy simply because it’s the most powerful iPad. Compare discounted M4 iPad Pro models, too: an older Pro could offer better value if its price is sufficiently below the equivalent M5 configuration. 
U.S. Black Friday price:  During October Prime Day, the 11-inch M5 iPad Pro with 256GB was $1,099, saving $100. So far we’re seeing nearly $300 off a 1TB 11-inch iPad Pro.
U.K. Black Friday price: October Prime Day brought little to recommend on the M5 iPad Pro, with reductions of around £12. Last Black Friday, older M4 iPad Pro offers included a saving of up to £200. AO is selling the 1TB 11-inch iPad Pro for £1,649. 
Apple’s deal: You can get a $125/£100 Apple Gift Card with an 11-inch or 13-inch M5 iPad Pro.






iPad (A16) – Our budget choice, at the right price

				
					

				
			
Apple




The A16 iPad remains a capable option for browsing, streaming, schoolwork, and everyday use. However, Apple raised its starting price by $100/£100 in June, and it doesn’t support Apple Intelligence.
That makes the final purchase price particularly important. A modest discount from today’s higher asking price may still leave you paying more than this iPad previously cost. With a replacement expected early in 2027, we’d look for a substantial Black Friday saving and compare the price with discounted iPad Air models before buying.
U.S. Black Friday price: This Black Friday, we are seeing $70 off the 128GB iPad. The current $379 price is lower than October’s $399 price. The 512GB iPad is £100 off at Amazon.
U.K. Black Friday price: October coverage listed the 256GB model at £499.97, around £29 off. Last Black Friday, the 128GB version was £299 and the 256GB version was £399. We hope to see even lower prices this year, but so far Amazon has the 128GB model for £399 and the 256GB model for £499, both £30 off. 






iPad mini with A20 Pro – Best for portability

				
					

				
			
Apple




The new iPad mini went on sale on November 6, replacing the A17 Pro model. It brings an 8.5-inch OLED display, the A20 Pro chip, and a thinner, lighter design, making it the option to consider if you want a compact iPad with the latest hardware.
Because it has only just arrived, we’d expect initial discounts to be smaller than clearance savings on its predecessor. The older A17 Pro mini could still be worthwhile at a sufficiently low price, but compare the saving with what you give up – particularly the new display.
U.S. Black Friday price: The A20 Pro mini wasn’t available during October Prime Day or last Black Friday. Amazon has it for $599, $100 off and the best price we’ve seen so far. Its 128GB A17 Pro predecessor was $499 during October Prime Day and $399 last Black Friday. Should you buy an iPad now or wait for a better deal?

				
					

				
			
There’s an iPad for everyone.

Foundry




With Black Friday approaching, we’d avoid paying full price unless you need an iPad immediately. But sales stretch across much of November, so an early offer can be worth taking if the price is competitive. Compare the exact generation, screen size, storage, and connectivity rather than waiting for Black Friday simply because a larger discount might appear.
If you’re buying an iPad Air and already plan to buy an Apple Pencil or keyboard later, Apple’s gift card may be worth waiting for. For the iPad Pro, check retailer prices first. The 11-inch M5 iPad Pro with 1TB has been listed at $299.01 off in the U.S. and £150 off in the U.K. at Amazon, both bigger savings than the Apple Gift Card.
Previous selling prices are particularly important this year because Apple raised iPad prices in June. During October Prime Day, the 128GB A16 iPad was $399, while the 11-inch M4 iPad Air with 128GB was $649. Both were discounted against Apple’s increased prices, but cost more than their regular prices before June. A saving from today’s asking price doesn’t necessarily mean you’re getting an exceptional bargain.
For the M4 iPad Air and M5 iPad Pro, we’d focus on finding a good price: We don’t expect replacements until 2027, as explained in our guide to the best time to buy an iPad. We’d be more cautious about the A16 iPad, which lacks Apple Intelligence and is expected to be replaced. Unless you find a substantial saving, waiting could get you a more capable entry-level model.
The new A20 Pro iPad mini has already seen price drops. In the U.S., the 128GB iPad mini (A20 Pro) is already down to $599, $100 off its $699 MSRP. That’s the deal we’d pick if you want the latest model. The older128GB iPad mini (A17 Pro) is $499 if you’d rather save another $100. In the U.K., the new iPad mini still starts at its full £699 price, so if you’re buying for the discount, we’d wait.






Should you buy an older iPad? 

				
					

				
			
Foundry




An older iPad can be a good buy if its price reflects its age and the features you give up. Compare its actual selling price with the discounted price of its replacement, matching screen size, storage, and connectivity where possible. A large saving from an old launch price doesn’t necessarily make it better value.
The M3 iPad Air and M4 iPad Pro are worth considering at substantial clearance discounts. Both remain capable options, and you may get more benefit from a lower price or additional storage than from the latest processor. However, if the newer equivalent costs only slightly more, the saving may not justify choosing the older generation.
The A17 Pro iPad mini also deserves consideration now that the A20 Pro model has arrived. It supports Apple Intelligence and remains a capable compact tablet, but you miss the newer model’s OLED display, faster processor, and thinner, lighter design. We’d want a meaningful saving rather than a small reduction from its former asking price.
Be more cautious with much older models. Check whether they support the current version of iPadOS and the apps and features you need. Compatibility today doesn’t guarantee how many future software upgrades they’ll receive. Apple Intelligence support also varies: don’t assume every older Air, Pro, or mini includes it.
If you already own an Apple Pencil or keyboard, check compatibility before changing generations. Keeping compatible accessories could make an older iPad better value, while replacing them could erase part of your saving. Our iPad buying guide explains the differences between the ranges.






iPad deals to avoid
Check the exact configuration before comparing offers. Retailer listings can emphasize iPad, Air, or Pro without making the generation obvious. Confirm the chip, screen size, storage capacity, and whether you’re buying Wi-Fi or Wi-Fi + Cellular. A cheaper listing may be a different model rather than a better deal.
Don’t let a large advertised discount tempt you into paying for storage or connectivity you won’t use. A heavily reduced high-capacity or cellular iPad can still cost more than a simpler configuration that meets your needs. Compare the final purchase prices, rather than assuming the biggest saving represents the best value.
Check whether the price includes nano-texture glass, too. This optional finish (on the 1TB and 2TB M5 iPad Pro and the 256GB and 512GB A20 Pro iPad mini) reduces glare and makes fingerprints and oily smudges less noticeable, which can be useful if reflections make your iPad difficult to see in bright rooms or outdoors. It avoids much of the washed-out appearance associated with ordinary matte finishes, but contrast can drop at some viewing angles and the surface may be more scratch-sensitive. Availability depends on the model and storage configuration, so you could end up paying for both the finish and additional storage. If reflections rarely bother you, standard glass may be better value. Read our guide to nano-texture glass and whether you need it.
Our iPad buying guide considers cellular a luxury for most buyers. If you mainly use your iPad somewhere with Wi-Fi, you may get little benefit from the extra hardware. For occasional use elsewhere, sharing your iPhone’s connection through Personal Hotspot can be a more economical option.
Cellular makes more sense if you regularly need an independent connection while commuting or traveling; it also adds built-in GPS for accurate location tracking. Factor in any data-plan charges and compare the total cost of a contract with buying outright. A cellular model can still be worthwhile if its sale price matches or beats the equivalent Wi-Fi version—you don’t have to activate a data plan simply because the hardware is included.
Judge savings against previous selling prices as well as Apple’s current price. Following June’s price increases, a discounted iPad may still cost more than it did earlier in the year. Also distinguish a cash discount from a gift-card offer: a gift card doesn’t reduce the amount you pay for the iPad and is useful only if you’ll spend it.
Check what any bundle includes. A keyboard, case, or stylus doesn’t automatically make an offer better value, particularly if the accessories aren’t the versions you want. Read the conditions attached to “free” iPads, trade-in promotions, contracts, and rebates before comparing their total cost with buying outright.
Finally, check whether the iPad is new, refurbished, or used, who is selling it, and what warranty and returns policy apply. For used or refurbished models, look for information about battery condition and confirm that Activation Lock has been removed. Be cautious about devices that remain tied to a previous owner or an organization’s management system.






How we choose iPad deals
Macworld’s editors have decades of experience with Apple devices, and our recommendations draw on hands-on iPad reviews and everyday use. We consider performance, display quality, portability, battery life, and accessory support alongside price to explain which iPads suit different buyers.
Our reviews help us assess whether paying more brings practical benefits. A faster processor or premium display may matter for demanding creative work, while a less expensive iPad can be perfectly capable of browsing, streaming, and schoolwork. We also consider the cost of keyboards, Apple Pencils, and other accessories when judging an iPad’s value.
We combine those findings with current prices and previous offers, matching the generation, screen size, storage, and connectivity so that comparisons reflect what you’re actually buying. Following Apple’s June price increases, we also consider earlier selling prices rather than relying solely on savings against today’s recommended price.
Older models can be worthwhile clearance purchases, but only when their prices make sense alongside newer alternatives. Our iPad buying guide explains the differences between the ranges, while our purchase-timing guide helps you decide whether to buy now or wait.

title: Apple is running macOS on an iPad, but you won't be able to
content:
Apple has macOS running on iPads internally, but despite the existence of the cross-platform experiment, it's far from becoming a reality for users anytime soon.


macOS on an iPad would make the tablet be even more like a notebook. 
The idea of having an iPad that runs on macOS has been a dream scenario for some Mac users, but it has never officially become a reality. However, while the public isn't getting access to such a device in the foreseeable future, Apple is already experimenting with it.
Answering a listener's question on his "Power On" podcast for Bloomberg, Mark Gurman says that Apple has iPads running macOS internally. Apple apparently, and perhaps obviously, has been running it for a while already.

Which Apple Watch should you buy this Black Friday?


Apple Watch Series 12 – Our best overall choice

				
					

				
			

Apple




The Series 12 is the Apple Watch we recommend for most people. It combines Apple’s new Health Sensing System, more frequent heart-rate measurements, a Readiness score, and a tougher display with up to 24 hours of battery life.
A worthwhile Black Friday discount could make it an attractive purchase, but compare it with remaining Series 11 stock. The older model has the same quoted battery life, so a substantial saving may outweigh the newer health features.

Apple Watch Ultra 4 – Best for battery life and outdoor adventures

				
					

				
			

Apple




The Ultra 4 is our choice for endurance athletes, outdoor enthusiasts, and buyers who prioritize battery life. It offers up to 50 hours of normal use, satellite communication, precision dual-frequency GPS, diving features, and Apple’s new Health Sensing System.
It’s more watch than most people need. Compare it with the Ultra 3, though, which retains many of its outdoor features but has a shorter 42-hour battery-life rating.

Apple Watch SE 3 – Our best budget choice

It remains part of Apple’s current lineup despite launching in 2025. A strong Black Friday offer could make it an excellent affordable purchase, although its previous discounts mean there’s little reason to settle for a token reduction.

Apple




The Ultra 3 is worth considering if you want a rugged Apple Watch without paying for the latest model. It offers satellite communication, dual-frequency GPS, diving features, and up to 42 hours of battery life.
You give up the Ultra 4’s longer battery life and newer Health Sensing System. Compare their actual selling prices: the Ultra 3 needs to be sufficiently cheaper to justify choosing the older generation.

Should you buy an Apple Watch now or wait for a better deal?
With Black Friday approaching, we’d avoid paying full price unless you need an Apple Watch immediately. But sales stretch across much of November, so you don’t necessarily need to wait for Black Friday itself. If an early offer matches or comes close to a previous low for the same model and configuration, it can be worth taking – particularly if you want a specific size, color, or band combination.
U.S. We’d buy now at the prices we are seeing for Black Friday. Amazon has the Apple Watch Series 12 GPS for $299 in 42mm and $349 in 46mm, down from $349 and $399 during October Prime Day. The SE 3 GPS is $179 in 40mm and $209 in 44mm, down from $199 and $229 in October. The Ultra 4 is $699, $75 below its October Prime Day price of $774.
U.K. Amazon’s £199 price for the 40mm Apple Watch SE 3 GPS matches its October Prime Day deal. The 44mm model is £223, £6 below its October price of £229. If you want the larger screen, it’s £24 more than the 40mm model at these prices.
Compare retailers, too. Last Black Friday, Walmart offered $150 off the Series 10, while U.K. shoppers could find up to £130 off at Currys and £200 off the Ultra 2’s original price at Argos. Our guide to the best time to buy an Apple Watch has more advice on choosing when to purchase.






Should you buy an older Apple Watch?

				
					

				
			
David Price / Foundry




Don’t assume an older Apple Watch is a bad buy. The Series 11 and Ultra 3 are only one generation old and can make excellent purchases if they’re substantially cheaper than the Series 12 or Ultra 4. Both retain many of their replacements’ core features, although you miss the newer Health Sensing System and, with the Ultra 3, the Ultra 4’s longer battery life.
Compare actual selling prices, matching case size, material, connectivity, and band where possible. A $50 difference between a Series 11 and Series 12 may not be enough to justify giving up the newer model’s health features, whereas a substantially larger saving could change the calculation. A discounted Series 11 could also be worth considering alongside the SE 3 if a small premium gets you features you’ll use.
Be much more cautious with the Series 8, SE 2, and original Ultra: those models cannot run watchOS 27. The Series 9 is the oldest standard Apple Watch compatible with the latest software, while the Ultra 2 is the oldest supported Ultra and the SE 3 is the only supported SE. Missing the latest software doesn’t make an older watch unusable, but it makes it harder to recommend as a purchase today.
The Series 9, Series 10, and Ultra 2 can still be worth considering at sufficiently low prices. However, compatibility with today’s software doesn’t guarantee how many future upgrades they’ll receive. Weigh the savings against the watch’s age and features, rather than assuming every supported generation offers equally good value.






Apple Watch deals to avoid 

				
					

				
			
David Price / Foundry




Don’t let a bigger advertised discount tempt you into paying more for a cellular Apple Watch you won’t use. If your iPhone is usually nearby, a GPS model can already handle calls, messages, and notifications through your phone. It can also track runs, use Apple Pay, and play downloaded music without your iPhone. As our experience testing a cellular Apple Watch showed, the extra connectivity may add little to everyday use.
Cellular is worth considering if you regularly leave your iPhone behind and want to remain contactable without Wi-Fi, or you’re setting up a watch for a child without an iPhone. Otherwise, you could pay extra for the hardware and then add an ongoing mobile-plan charge for a feature you rarely need. You don’t have to activate a plan on a cellular model, so it can still be a good buy if its sale price matches or beats the GPS version. Our GPS versus cellular Apple Watch guide explains the trade-offs.
Check the rest of the configuration, too. A premium case material or expensive band can make a heavily discounted watch cost more than a simpler version that meets your needs. Judge offers against previous selling prices as well as the advertised reduction: a large saving from the original launch price doesn’t necessarily mean exceptional value. Check any spending requirements, contracts, trade-ins, or rebates attached to offers advertising a “free” Apple Watch.
Finally, check whether you’re buying a new, refurbished, or used watch, who is selling it, and what warranty and returns policy apply. For a used or refurbished model, check the stated battery condition and confirm that it has been removed from the previous owner’s account, with Activation Lock turned off. Make sure the watch is compatible with your iPhone before ordering.






How we choose Apple Watch deals
Macworld’s editors have decades of experience with Apple devices, and our recommendations draw on hands-on Apple Watch reviews and everyday wear. We consider comfort, performance, battery life, charging, health and fitness features, and value – not just the specifications or advertised saving.
Our testing helps us explain which features are worth paying for. For example, our Series 12 review assessed battery life and charging performance alongside its newer health features. We also draw on everyday experience: our cellular Apple Watch testing examines whether staying connected without an iPhone justified the extra hardware and subscription costs.
We combine those findings with current prices and previous lows to judge whether an offer represents good value. We check the generation, case size, material, connectivity, and included band so that comparisons reflect what you’re actually buying. Older models can be worthwhile clearance purchases, but only when their prices make sense alongside discounted replacements.
Our Best Apple Watch guide explains why the most expensive model isn’t necessarily the right choice: your budget, wrist size, activities, and the features you need all matter.

title: Apple Has iPads Running macOS Internally, Says Gurman
content:
Apple has iPads running macOS internally and has had them "for some time," according to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman, although he says no work is currently being done to bring the Mac operating system to iPads.

Power On podcast, Gurman said there is "no work being done to consumerize macOS on the iPad." Rather, Apple will continue to bring Mac features and apps like Final Cut to iPadOS piece by piece. Gurman also argued that per-operating-system EU regulation gives Apple an incentive to keep distinct systems for each device. Apple recently dismissed merging iPadOS and macOS.

Apple's busiest season isn't over yet – far from it. With Black Friday kicking off this week, plus new products, software updates, and new smart home accessories running into December, there's more on the way from Apple before the end of 2026, so be sure to stick around.


Below, we've rounded up what's still coming, along with one date in particular that's worth watching if you're a holiday shopper.


Black Friday – November 27: Not a product launch unfortunately, but a date likely worth marking. Apple's annual four-day shopping event runs from Friday, November 27 through Monday, November 30, with gift cards worth up to $300 offered with eligible purchases. Apple is also offering new and qualified returning subscribers the Apple TV streaming service for $6.99 per month for six months, with that deal available until November 30. Our Black Friday roundup will be tracking all the deals.

(PRODUCT)RED AirPods Max 2 and HomePod mini 2 – expected December 1: Apple plans to release (PRODUCT)RED versions of the existing AirPods Max 2 and HomePod mini 2 on or around Tuesday, December 1, which is World AIDS Day, according to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman. The new color is expected to be the only change. Apple is also releasing a red Wrist Strap for AirPods Pro and a red Sport Band for the Apple Watch.

App Store Awards – expected December: Apple named this year's finalists on November 18, and the winners are expected in the coming weeks. Last year, Apple announced the winners on December 4, so a similar early-December date looks likely this year.

Apple Music Replay – expected December: The full 2026 Replay recap is likely to arrive around the same time as last year's, when the full version became available on December 2, with your top songs, artists, and listening stats for the year.

iOS 27.3 – December: Apple says iOS 27.3 will be released to the public in December, though it hasn't given a date. The first iOS 27.3 beta arrived on Tuesday, November 3. Beta features can change before release, but so far it includes new Siri AI actions across apps, vertical tabs and an Adaptive Dark Mode in Safari, the redesigned Health app, a new Apple Fitness+ Gym Strength workout that builds a four-week plan, and more. Our iOS 27.3 beta guide has the full list.

Apple Intelligence in China – December: The first Apple Intelligence features for users in China are already in testing in the iOS 27.3 beta, and Apple has confirmed the public rollout for December alongside the update. Apple has partnered with Alibaba to add Qwen support to Siri, Writing Tools, and Visual Intelligence. The initial release is for supported iPhones, with other platforms to follow after the required regulatory approvals, and it does not include Siri AI.

Apple Home Collection – from December: The new Apple-backed, third-party lineup includes smart home cameras, thermostats, and a lock designed with LG Electronics and Schneider Electric. Apple says that availability begins in December, although select accessories will not arrive until early 2027.

This article, "Apple Is Far From Done With 2026: Here's What's Still Coming" first appeared on MacRumors.com

title: My favorite running earbuds aren’t AirPods—and they’ll only cost you $17 right now
content:
Macworld





		
JLab Go Sport+ wireless earbuds for 42% off
View Deal
Getting fit is all about motivation, particularly as the nights get colder. And one of the best ways to stay motivated during a winter running session is to blast high-energy beats through a good pair of headphones.
But how do we define good? The criteria are a little different for running headphones. Audio performance focuses more on the bass end. Quality of fit needs to be exceptional. And, given that they’re going to be subjected to sweat, rain, and the threat of loss or even theft, it’s best to choose a cheaper and altogether more replaceable set than your $249 AirPods Pro.
I’ve written elsewhere about my struggles to find the perfect running headphones for my needs, and how I eventually settled on the JLab Go Sport+ wireless earbuds. Thanks to the rubber ear hooks, they’ve never yet fallen off my head; the audio quality is solid, and at just under $30 they’re excellent value. But with Black Friday approaching, I’m happy to report that they’ve just become even more irresistible.
On Amazon right now, you can buy the JLab Go Sport+ earbuds in Graphite for just $17, a whopping 42 percent off an already appealing MSRP. They’ve never dropped that low before. It’s an absolutely unmissable deal.
The only piece of advice I’d offer before you rush to click the buy button is to consider one of the other colors. I own the light blue set, which are rather jolly and costs $22.39 at the moment. But my suggestion would be the magnificent yellow set, which I’ve long had my eye on (currently $20.99), or the glorious Coral option at $18.52. As I’ve said before, one of the nicest things about budget tech like this is that you don’t actually have to choose. You can afford to buy two different colors and alternate them depending on your mood.
For more advice, check out our guide to the best Apple Black Friday deals, and our guide to the best wireless earbuds.

PRICES CHECKED NOVEMBER 25, 2026 – Deals change quickly, so we will update this page throughout November.
Black Friday is one of the best opportunities to save on a Mac, with retailers competing to discount MacBooks and desktop models – including recently released machines. The Black Friday Mac deals are already here, and the 13-inch M5 MacBook Air with 512GB of storage is where we’d start for most people. Amazon has listed it for $1,049 in the U.S. and £1,148.97 in the U.K., saving $250 and about £150 off Apple’s current prices. If you already have a display, keyboard, and mouse, the M6 Mac mini is a cheaper way to get a new Mac at $779 or £759.
There are bigger savings on MacBook Pro models if you need the extra power. In the U.S., Amazon has listed the 14-inch M5 Max MacBook Pro with 36GB of memory and 2TB of storage for $3,599, $500 off. In the U.K., the 16-inch M5 Pro MacBook Pro with 24GB of memory and 1TB of storage is £2,599, £400 off. That’s about £536 less than the equivalent touchscreen model on sale, so think about how much you’d benefit from the OLED display before paying the premium.
Apple’s June price increases make the advertised savings worth a closer look. The U.S. MacBook Air deal is $50 below its pre-increase price, while the U.K. offer is still about £50 above what Apple charged before June. We compare prices for the same configurations so you can see which deals are worth taking and which have been better before.
Below, we explain which Mac to buy at these prices, from the budget MacBook Neo to the Mac Studio. If you’re deciding whether to buy now or wait for Apple’s November 27–30 promotion, compare what you’d pay today with what you’d actually use from a gift card on a future purchase. For more offers, visit our Black Friday coverage and our Apple Black Friday deals roundups of the best iPad deals, Apple Watch deals and AirPods deals.
Apple Store Black Friday offer: From November 27 to 30, Apple is offering a gift card worth $200/£160 with either size of M5 MacBook Air, $250/£200 with an eligible 14-inch M5 Pro or M5 Max MacBook Pro, $300/£240 with an eligible 16-inch M5 Pro or M5 Max MacBook Pro, and $100/£80 with an eligible Mac mini. The gift card is for a future Apple purchase. Compare its value with the upfront discounts we share below. See the full Apple Black Friday offer.
Which Mac or MacBook should you buy this Black Friday?


MacBook Air – Our best overall choice 

				
					

				
			
Ida Blix




The MacBook Air is our recommendation for most buyers. Both sizes offer a lightweight, silent laptop for everyday work, studying, and occasional creative projects. Choose the 13-inch for portability or the 15-inch for more workspace without MacBook Pro pricing.
We’d prioritize a competitive price on the memory and storage you need. For regular lengthy exports or other sustained demanding tasks, consider a MacBook Pro with active cooling instead.
U.S. Black Friday price: October Prime Day brought the 13-inch M5 Air with 16GB memory and 512GB storage to $1,099, and the equivalent 15-inch to $1,299. We are already seeing up to $300 off the 13-inch models, and $300 off the 15-inch options, bringing the price below the original MSRP from before Apple increased prices. These savings are better than Apple’s $200 gift card.
U.K. Black Friday price: October offers included approximately £1,199 for the 13-inch M5 Air and £1,349 for the 15-inch, both with 512GB storage. Last Black Friday’s M4 models with 256GB reached £849 and £1,025. Match storage capacities when comparing generations. Amazon has the 13-inch M5 MacBook Air with 512GB of storage, 16GB of memory, and an 8-core GPU for £1,148.97, saving £150 off Apple’s £1,299 price. That’s about £50 less than it cost during October Prime Day. Amazon also has the 15-inch M5 MacBook Air with 512GB of storage and 16GB of memory for £1,299, saving £200 off Apple’s £1,499 price. Earlier in November, we saw a larger £200 discount on the 13-inch MacBook Air.
The £160 Apple gift card is close to the £150 upfront discount on the 13-inch 512GB Air.
Apple’s Deal: Apple’s £160 gift card is worth about £10 more than Amazon’s upfront discount on the 13-inch model. On the 15-inch model, Amazon’s upfront discount is £40 more than the gift card’s value.






MacBook Neo – Our budget choice, at the right price

				
					

				
			
Eugen Wegmann




The MacBook Neo suits browsing, schoolwork, streaming, and office apps. Its lower starting price makes it appealing, but its fixed 8GB of memory leaves less room for demanding workloads.
Check which configuration is discounted: only the 512GB version includes Touch ID. Both lack a backlit keyboard, MagSafe, and Thunderbolt. Compare clearance MacBook Air stock before deciding how much those compromises save you.
U.S. Black Friday price: Amazon has the 256GB MacBook Neo for $649 ($50 off) and the 512GB model with Touch ID for $749 ($50 off).
U.K. Black Friday price: The 256GB MacBook Neo is £679.97 (£19.03 off), and the 512GB model with Touch ID is £766 (£33 off).






MacBook Pro M6 – Best step up from the Air

				
					

				
			
Macbook Pro M6 Aufmacher

Halyna Kubiv




The standard M6 MacBook Pro is worth considering if you want a better built-in display, more connections, and cooling for sustained workloads without paying for a Pro or Max chip. It comes in a 14-inch size, with a non-touch Liquid Retina XDR display, HDMI, and an SDXC card slot.
It starts with 16GB memory and 1TB storage, so account for those specifications when comparing prices with an Air or older Pro. Despite the newer generation number, the standard M6 isn’t automatically the better choice for demanding work than an M5 Pro or M5 Max.
U.S. Black Friday price: The M6 model wasn’t available during October Prime Day, but it’s on offer for Black Friday with $200 off at Amazon, where it’s $1,799. B&H also has $150 off the 14-inch MacBook Pro (M6)
U.K. Black Friday price: Last Black Friday, the older 14-inch M5 with 16GB memory and 1TB storage reached approximately £1,619. Amazon has the 14-inch M6 MacBook Pro with 16GB of memory and 1TB of storage for £1,829.97, saving £169.03. That’s just £30.97 more than the equivalent M5 model at £1,799, so we’d buy the M6.






MacBook Pro M5 Pro – Best for demanding professional work

				
					

				
			
Foundry




The non-touchscreen M5 Pro MacBook Pro is a strong choice for development, photography, video editing, and heavier multitasking. Available in 14-inch and 16-inch sizes, it offers professional performance without the Max chip’s higher price.
Compare it with the touchscreen version using the same memory and storage. Both offer M5 Pro configurations, so a discounted non-touch model could be particularly good value if its existing XDR display meets your needs.
U.S. Black Friday price: October prices included $2,339 for the 14-inch M5 Pro with 24GB memory and 1TB storage, and $2,749 for the equivalent 16-inch. So far this Black Friday month we are seeing $256 off the 16-inch MacBook Pro with M5 Pro and $250 off the 14-inch MacBook Pro with M5 Pro. Note that Amazon takes $250 off upfront while Apple offers $250 or $300 (depending on the model) in future credit, so it might be worth waiting for Apple’s deal if you are likely to want to make future Apple purchases.
U.K. Black Friday price: The equivalent configurations reached approximately £2,250 and £2,700. Last Black Friday, selected previous-generation M4 Pro models received discounts of around £350. The 16-inch MacBook Pro (M5 Pro, 24GB memory, 1TB SSD) is £2,599 (£400 off at Amazon). In that case, the £400 Amazon discount beats Apple’s £240 Gift card offer in the U.K.

MacBook Pro M5 Max – Best for demanding graphics and video

				
					

				
			
Ida Blix




Consider the non-touchscreen M5 Max MacBook Pro if your work benefits from additional graphics power or more memory than an M5 Pro supports. Complex 3D projects and demanding video production make a stronger case for it than everyday productivity.
We’d choose the configuration around the work you do. A larger advertised discount on a Max doesn’t necessarily make it better value than a less expensive Pro that meets your needs. Our MacBook Pro buying advice explains the options.

Touchscreen MacBook Pro – Best for its OLED display

				
					

				
			


Roman Loyola/Foundry




The touchscreen MacBook Pro is most compelling for its OLED display and thinner, lighter design. Improved blacks and reduced blooming could matter more to your everyday experience than touch controls, particularly if you spend most of your working day using the built-in screen.
Available in 14-inch and 16-inch sizes with M5 Pro or M5 Max chips, these models offer comparable processing performance to their non-touch equivalents. Compare matching configurations: the regular premium is $400/£400, so consider how much you’ll benefit from the display before paying extra.

Foundry




The M6 Mac mini suits buyers who already own a display, keyboard, and mouse. It offers a compact desktop for everyday work and lighter creative projects. Check storage carefully: the entry-level model has a restrictive 256GB SSD.
U.S. Black Friday price: October’s entry-level M6 mini reached approximately $780. Last Black Friday, the older M4 equivalent was $479. So far this November we’ve seen $150 off the 512GB model.

Mac mini M5 Pro – Best compact desktop for professional work

The M5 Pro mini offers more processing power and memory capacity for demanding work without moving to a Studio. Compare upgraded configurations carefully: if the total approaches Mac Studio pricing, check which machine better suits your workload.

iMac – Best complete desktop setup

				
					

				
			

Foundry




The iMac combines a 24-inch 4.5K display with the computer and matching accessories. Compare the two-port and four-port versions carefully: the latter adds processing power, connections, and a Touch ID keyboard. Factor those differences into the final price.
U.S. Black Friday price: The M6 wasn’t available during October Prime Day. The entry-level M4 predecessor reached approximately $1,360 in October and $1,149 last Black Friday. We are seeing $74 off the iMac M6 at Amazon.

Mac Studio – Best for demanding desktop workflows

				
					

				
			
Stephan Wiesend




The M5 Max Studio suits demanding graphics, video, and other professional workloads. Compare it with the M5 Pro mini first. The considerably more expensive M5 Ultra is for exceptional workloads requiring its additional performance and memory; most buyers won’t need it. Budget for a display and peripherals.

Should you buy a Mac or MacBook now or wait for a better deal?
With Black Friday approaching, we’d avoid paying full price unless you need a Mac immediately. But sales stretch across much of November, so an early offer can be worth taking if it matches or approaches a previous low for the same configuration. Waiting can be a gamble if you’re buying clearance stock with a particular screen size, memory capacity, or finish. If the retailer discount is close to Apple’s gift card value and you already have another Apple purchase planned, it may be worth waiting until November 27 to take advantage of Apple’s gift card offer, but note that MacBook Neo, standard M6 MacBook Pro, iMac and Mac Studio are not included in Apple’s Black Friday deal. 
The M5 MacBook Air remains an appealing purchase at a good discount, with a replacement not expected until 2027. The recently updated Mac mini and Mac Studio are also worth considering if they meet your needs. The main reason to wait is a better price rather than an imminent replacement.
MacBook Pro buyers no longer need to wait for the rumored October launches: the standard M6 and OLED touchscreen models are now available. However, their recent arrival may limit initial discounts. Non-touch M5 Pro and M5 Max models could offer better value, particularly if you don’t need the touchscreen version’s improved display and lighter design. If your existing M4 or M5 MacBook Pro still meets your needs, there’s little reason to upgrade simply because a newer option exists.
The M6 iMac has only just arrived, replacing the aging M4 version. Compare a modest saving on the latest model with a substantial clearance discount on its predecessor, rather than assuming the older machine is automatically the better deal.
Previous prices need context this year. Following June’s increases, a discount from Apple’s current asking price may still leave you paying more than before the increases. Compare retailers as well: Amazon competes with Best Buy, Walmart, and B&H in the U.S., and retailers including Currys and John Lewis in the U.K. Our MacBook Pro buying advice explains the current choices.






Which Mac specifications are worth paying for?
The cheapest Mac isn’t always the best value. Use Black Friday to get a configuration that will serve you for longer within your budget, but don’t pay for performance or features you won’t use.
Check the exact chip, screen size, memory, and storage. A standard M6 and an M5 Pro or M5 Max serve different needs: the newer generation number alone doesn’t tell you which is better for your work. For MacBook Pro listings, distinguish the OLED touchscreen version from non-touch models.
Avoid saving a small amount by buying too little memory or storage. Most current Macs start with 16GB of unified memory, but the MacBook Neo has a fixed 8GB, and some desktop configurations include only a 256GB SSD. Unified memory cannot be upgraded later. An external SSD can add storage, but it cannot compensate for insufficient RAM.
Once the processor meets your needs, additional memory may be more useful than a faster chip. Compare a discounted Air with the Neo, too: the M5 Air starts with twice the memory and storage of the entry-level Neo. Our Mac buying guide explains which specifications suit different workloads.
Check whether the configuration includes nano-texture glass. This optional finish reduces glare and reflections, which can help in bright rooms or near windows, but increases the price. If reflections rarely bother you, standard glass may offer better value.






Should you buy an older Mac or MacBook?

				
					

				
			
Foundry




An older Mac can be excellent value if its price reflects its age and configuration. Compare its actual selling price with the discounted price of the newer equivalent, rather than focusing on a large percentage saving from its original launch price.
Previous-generation Apple silicon models are the most promising starting point. A discounted M4 MacBook Air or standard M5 MacBook Pro may meet your needs comfortably. Older Pro and Max configurations can also be worth considering if they provide the memory, graphics performance, and connections your work requires for substantially less money.
Check what the saving buys—and what you give up. An older Mac with more memory or storage could be more useful than a newer entry-level configuration. Conversely, a cheaper older Air with 256GB storage isn’t directly comparable with an M5 Air that starts with 512GB. The non-touch M5 Pro and M5 Max MacBook Pros also remain current options, despite the arrival of the standard M6 and touchscreen models.
Be much more cautious with Intel Macs. Their software support is winding down, and a low purchase price may leave you with a machine that has a limited useful life for current apps and macOS features. Check compatibility with the software you need before buying any older model.
For used or refurbished Macs, check battery condition on laptops, warranty coverage, and the returns policy. Confirm that Activation Lock has been removed and that the Mac isn’t still enrolled in an organization’s management system.
For more advice read:
Should I buy a MacBook Neo?
Should I buy a MacBook Air?
Should I buy a MacBook Pro?
Should I buy a Mac mini?
Should I buy a Mac Studio?






Mac or MacBook deals to avoid
Treat large advertised discounts carefully. Following June’s price increases, “$400 off” may simply bring a Mac closer to what it cost before the increase. Compare previous selling prices for the same configuration, rather than judging the offer solely against today’s recommended price.
Check whether the price includes AppleCare+ or another protection plan. Some Amazon listings bundle coverage with the Mac. If you don’t want it, a listing without coverage could be cheaper; if you do, compare the bundle with buying the Mac and coverage separately.
Check for a bundled power adapter, too. Some Mac laptops are sold without one in the U.K. and EU. A charger bundle may be useful if you need an adapter, but could mean paying extra unnecessarily if you already own a suitable one.
Compare the complete setup cost. A Mac mini or Studio requires a display, keyboard, and mouse or trackpad, while adapters and docks can add to the cost of any Mac.
Finally, distinguish cash discounts from gift cards, trade-ins, financing, and membership-only offers. Read the conditions, check the seller, and confirm whether the Mac is new, refurbished, or used, along with its warranty and returns policy.






How we choose Mac and MacBook deals
Macworld has covered the Mac since its launch in 1984, and our recommendations draw on decades of experience and hands-on reviews. We consider performance, display quality, battery life, portability, connectivity, and everyday use alongside price to explain which Macs suit different buyers.
Our reviews help us assess which upgrades are worth paying for. We look at whether additional processing power benefits demanding workloads, when more memory is useful, and whether a premium display justifies the extra cost. A MacBook Air may offer better value for everyday work, while a Pro, Max, or Ultra configuration needs to earn its higher price through the work it enables.
We combine those findings with current prices and previous offers, matching the exact chip, screen size, memory, and storage. Following Apple’s June price increases, we also consider earlier selling prices rather than judging a deal solely against today’s recommended retail price. A large advertised discount doesn’t automatically make an offer exceptional.
We consider the complete purchase, too: the retailer, product condition, warranty, and any conditions attached to the price. For desktop Macs, we also account for the display and accessories you’ll need. Our Mac buying guide and MacBook comparison explain how to choose the right model and configuration.
