The Apple Watch Ultra 4 is Apple’s most capable watch, aimed at endurance athletes, hikers, divers and anyone who regularly spends more than a day away from a charger. It starts at $799/£749, the same starting price as the Ultra 3, and retains the 49mm titanium case, bright display, dual-frequency GPS, satellite communication and diving support. 
Battery life is the strongest reason to choose the new model. Apple rates the Ultra 4 for up to 50 hours of normal use, up from 42 hours on Ultra 3, or 84 hours in Low Power Mode, up from 72. Its new Extended Workout modes can track outdoor activity for up to 25 hours with full GPS and heart-rate readings, or up to 45 hours in Max Extended Workout mode. Like the Series 12, it gains the new Health Sensing System, more frequent heart-rate and HRV readings, and a Readiness score. Its S11 chip supports Audio Intelligence, although Live Rewind and Siri Recap are due in beta later in 2026. 
Buy the Apple Watch Ultra 4 if:
You want the longest battery life available on an Apple Watch, particularly for travel, long shifts or time away from a charger.
You need extended outdoor workout tracking, precision dual-frequency GPS or satellite communication.
You hike, dive or take part in endurance sports and will use its rugged case, Action button and specialist features.
You want the new Health Sensing System in an Ultra watch and are upgrading from a substantially older model.
Don’t buy the Apple Watch Ultra 4 if:
You already own an Ultra 3 and its 42-hour battery life meets your needs. It retains many of the same outdoor features, including satellite communication and dual-frequency GPS.
You find an Ultra 3 at a substantial discount and do not need the Ultra 4’s longer battery life, new health sensing or extended workout modes.
You mainly want advanced health features in an everyday watch. The smaller Series 12 has the same new Health Sensing System and S11 chip for half the starting price.
You prefer a smaller or lighter watch. The Ultra 4’s 49mm case can feel bulky, especially for sleep tracking.
Our verdict: The Ultra 4 is worth buying if you will benefit from its 50-hour battery life, extended workout tracking or outdoor safety features. It also offers the Series 12’s new health sensing in a more rugged watch. For everyday use, the Series 12 offers better value; if you already own an Ultra 3, compare the cost of upgrading with how much its extra eight hours of rated battery life and new health features matter to you. 

							
		


Should I buy an older Apple Watch?

				
					

				
			
Foundry




The Series 11 and Ultra 3 are now the previous-generation models and may be good buys if retailers discount them enough. Before choosing any older Apple Watch, check both its price against the current model and whether it can run watchOS 27. The Series 9 and Ultra 2 are the oldest supported Apple Watch models models in their respective ranges; the SE 3 is the only supported SE.
The following models cannot install watchOS 27, so we would generally avoid buying them unless the price is exceptionally low and you are comfortable using older software:
Apple Watch Series 6 (2020)
Apple Watch Series 7 (2021)
Apple Watch Series 8 (2022)
Apple Watch SE (2nd generation, 2022)
Apple Watch Ultra (1st generation, 2022)
Start by comparing a discounted Series 11 with the Series 12, or an Ultra 3 with the Ultra 4. The Series 11 retains the Series 12’s 24-hour everyday battery rating but lacks its new Health Sensing System and Audio Intelligence features. The Ultra 3 retains satellite communication and dual-frequency GPS, but its rated battery life is 42 hours rather than the Ultra 4’s 50 hours. Series 10 and Ultra 2 can offer further savings if their price and battery condition make sense; Series 9 is the oldest standard model that runs watchOS 27.
What to look for when buying an older Apple Watch
Choose an S9 chip or newer for the longest software support.
Buy refurbished if possible. Apple’s Certified Refurbished Store includes a one-year warranty, while reputable third-party refurbishers can also offer good value.
Shop during major sales. Previous-generation Apple Watches often receive their biggest discounts during Prime Day and Black Friday.
Check the battery and Activation Lock. If you’re buying used, confirm the battery is in good condition, inspect the watch for damage, and make sure Activation Lock has been removed before you buy.

When is the best time to buy an Apple Watch?
The best time to buy an Apple Watch depends on whether you want the newest model or the lowest price.
The Series 12 and Ultra 4 are now on sale, alongside the SE 3. If you want the latest model and are happy with its price, you can buy now without an imminent replacement to worry about. If getting a discount matters more, compare retailers during the expected October sales and Black Friday in November.
The September launch also makes the Series 11 and Ultra 3 worth checking. Retailers may reduce remaining stock, but compare the actual saving with the features you would give up: the Series 12 and Ultra 4 add new health sensing, while the Ultra 4 also increases rated battery life from 42 to 50 hours.
Apple kept the new models’ starting prices at $399/£369 for Series 12 and $799/£749 for Ultra 4. Individual configurations and retailer prices vary.


						

							


When shouldn’t you buy an Apple Watch?
Avoid buying an Apple Watch:
Just before Apple’s annual September event, unless you need one immediately.
At full price when a major sale is only days away, such as Prime Day or Black Friday.
Without comparing prices. Check multiple retailers and use price-tracking tools such as CamelCamelCamel to avoid inflated “sale” prices.
If you’re paying extra for cellular but don’t need it. Cellular Apple Watch typically cost around $100 more and require a monthly data plan, while the GPS model offers better value for most people.
If battery life is your top priority. Apple Watch battery life still trails some competing smartwatches, so you may prefer an alternative platform if multi-day battery life is essential.


						

							






Best time to buyWhy

Prime Day (July/October)Best deals on current-generation models.
Black Friday (November)Consistently some of the lowest prices of the year.
After the September launchPrevious-generation models receive substantial discounts.
Worst time: August to early SeptemberNew Apple Watches are expected within weeks.

 






Where to find the best Apple Watch deals

				
					

				
			
IDG




Apple rarely discounts the Apple Watch itself, so the best deals are usually found at third-party retailers – we check these every month and record the best deals here: Top Apple Watch discounts & deals – Big savings on all models.
Best places to buy: Amazon is consistently one of the best places to find Apple Watch discounts, particularly during major sales. Other good options in the U.S. include Best Buy, Walmart, Target and Costco. In the U.K., check Amazon, Currys, Argos, John Lewis and KRCS.
Shop during major sales: The biggest discounts typically arrive during Amazon Prime Day (July and October) and Black Friday/Cyber Monday (November). Savings of $100–$150 on current-generation models are common. During Prime Day 2026, for example, the Apple Watch Series 11 fell to $279 ($120 off) and the Ultra 3 dropped to $649 ($150 off).
Check for education discounts: Students, teachers and education staff may qualify for discounted Apple Watch pricing through Apple’s Education Store U.S. (and Education Store U.K.). For more information read our guide to how to get a student discount at the Apple Education Store.
Tip: Before buying, compare prices across several retailers and check the recent price history with a tool such as CamelCamelCamel to make sure you’re getting a genuine deal rather than a temporary “discount” from an inflated price.


						

							


Is it worth buying a refurbished Apple Watch?
Buying a refurbished Apple Watch is another great way to save money, provided you buy from a reputable seller and choose a model that will continue to receive software updates.
Apple’s Certified Refurbished Store is the safest option. Every watch undergoes rigorous testing, cleaning and inspection, comes with a one-year warranty, includes new accessories, and is eligible for AppleCare. Apart from the plain white box, it’s difficult to tell the difference between a refurbished Apple Watch and a brand-new one. You can typically save around 15% on recent models, with even bigger discounts on older generations.
Check Apple’s U.S. Refurbished Store or U.K. Refurbished Store for current models, configurations and prices. Stock changes regularly; compare any refurbished Series 11 or Ultra 3 with the price of a new Series 12 or Ultra 4 before buying.
The best Apple Watch refurbished deals: 
Apple’s U.S. Refurbished Store often has Apple Watch Series 11, 10 and 9, SE 3, SE 2, Ultra 2 and Ultra 3.
Get a refurbished Apple Watch Series 11 for $339, $60 off
You may also find the Apple Watch Series 11, 10 and 9, SE 2, SE 3 and Ultra 3 at Apple’s U.K. Refurbished Store. 
Get a refurbished Apple Watch Series 11 for £309, £60 off
Third-party refurbishers can also offer excellent value, but quality varies. Terms such as “Excellent” or “Grade A”aren’t standardised, so always check the seller’s warranty, return policy and battery condition before buying. Be aware that Amazon Renewed devices, for example, aren’t refurbished to Apple’s standards and may not include a new battery or replacement parts.
The other key consideration is software support. Older Apple Watches eventually stop receiving new versions of watchOS, so avoid buying a model that’s nearing the end of its supported life. For the best balance of price and features, compare refurbished Series 11 and Ultra 3 models with the new generation first. Series 9, Series 10 and Ultra 2 can cost less and still run watchOS 27, but check their condition and savings carefully.
A refurbished Apple Watch can be one of the best values in Apple’s lineup – as long as you buy from a trusted seller and don’t choose a model that’s too old.
Read: Should I buy a refurbished Apple Watch? for more information.


						

							





 FAQ 


1.
Should I wait for the next Apple Watch?
You do not need to wait for 2026’s launch: the Series 12 and Ultra 4 went on sale in September 2026, and the SE 3 remains in Apple’s lineup. If you need a watch now, choose the model that fits your needs and budget. If you are mainly looking for a lower price, consider waiting for a sale or comparing discounted Series 11 and Ultra 3 stock. 
Apple has not announced when the next Apple Watch models will arrive, but we expect that the next update will happen in September 2027.





2.
How long does Apple support an Apple Watch?
Apple has traditionally supported Apple Watches with major watchOS updates for around five to six years, but that changed with watchOS 27, announced at WWDC 2026.
Apple dropped support for five older models in a single release:
Apple Watch Series 6 (2020)
Apple Watch Series 7 (2021)
Apple Watch Series 8 (2022)
Apple Watch SE (2nd generation, 2022)
Apple Watch Ultra (1st generation, 2022)
As a result, watchOS 27 only supports Apple Watches with an S9 chip or later, starting with the Apple Watch Series 9. While Apple may continue to provide security updates for older models for a limited time, they no longer receive new watchOS features.
The change makes software support a much more important consideration when buying an older or refurbished Apple Watch. If you want the longest possible lifespan, choose a model with an S9 chip or newer.





3.
Is the Apple Watch Series 11 still worth buying?
If it is substantially cheaper than the Series 12. Both have up to 24 hours of rated everyday battery life, but the Series 12 adds more frequent heart-rate and HRV measurements, a Readiness score and support for upcoming Audio Intelligence features, so be sure that you are willing to give those features up for the saving.

Choosing the right Apple Watch depends on your budget, lifestyle and which features matter most to you. As of September 2026, Apple’s lineup consists of the Apple Watch Series 12, Apple Watch Ultra 4 and Apple Watch SE 3, although the various combinations of case size, material, color and band can make choosing one seem like a bit of a minefield.
The Apple Watch Series 12 is the best choice for most people, combining a tougher display and more advanced heart-rate sensing with an S11 chip and 24-hour battery life. The larger and more rugged Apple Watch Ultra 4 is designed for endurance sports and outdoor adventures, offering precision GPS, diving features and up to 50 hours of battery life. The Apple Watch SE 3 remains the best-value option for buyers who want the core Apple Watch experience and can live without features such as ECG and the latest health sensors.
Apple updated the Series and Ultra models in September 2026, but the SE was unchanged. However, the SE 3 only arrived in 2025 and includes significant improvements over its predecessor, including an always-on display, temperature sensing and the same S10 chip found in the Series 11. 
In this guide, we’ll explain the differences between the current models and help you decide whether you need to spend more on the Series 12 or Ultra 4 – or whether the SE 3 offers everything you need. We’ll compare their features, specifications and prices, as well as explain the choices of sizes, case materials, colors and bands, so you can buy the Apple Watch that best suits your needs.

The Apple Watch Series 12 is Apple’s mainstream premium smartwatch and the best choice for most people. Its S11 chip powers a redesigned heart-rate sensor system that measures your heart rate every five seconds throughout the day. It also enables Audio Intelligence features including Sound Recognition, Live Rewind and Siri Recap. Live Rewind and Siri Recap are available to test in the watchOS 27.3 beta. Both initially support English.
The design remains familiar, but Apple has introduced new finishes: Light Gold and Dark Bronze replace Silver and Rose Gold on aluminum models, while Radiant Gold replaces Gold on titanium versions. Ceramic cases also return in Night Blue and Pearl White. Prices still start at $399, although some configurations cost more than their Series 11 equivalents.
Key advantages and limitations
Aluminum models now use Ceramic Shield 2, which Apple claims is 60 percent more durable than the Ion-X glass used on the aluminum Series 11. Apple claims battery life remains at 24 hours, but outdoor workout tracking increases to 10 hours and the watch can charge to 80 percent in around 30 minutes.
In our Apple Watch Series 12 review, we recorded 51 and 40 hours of battery life across two runs – an average of 45.5 hours, compared with 47.5 hours for Series 11. Charging also varied: our Apple Watch Series 12 reached 58% and 72% after 30 minutes in separate tests, falling short of Apple’s claimed 80%. These results show that endurance can comfortably exceed Apple’s 24-hour rating, but they don’t demonstrate a consistent improvement over Series 11. Actual battery life depends on usage.
In the watchOS 27.3 beta, Live Rewind displays the previous 15 seconds of speech as text when you double-press the Digital Crown. However, assigning that gesture to Live Rewind means the traditional App Switcher is no longer available, making multitasking less convenient. The Series 12 also lacks the Ultra 4’s satellite connectivity, 50-hour battery life and brighter, more rugged display.
Who should buy the Apple Watch Series 12?
The Series 12 is the best option for anyone who wants Apple’s latest health and smart features without the size or price of the Ultra 4. Its advanced heart-rate sensing, Readiness score, tougher display and relatively compact design make it particularly attractive to health-conscious users and anyone upgrading from a Series 9 or older.
The new health features make Series 12 worth considering, but our review found variable battery life and charging, plus occasional sluggishness. Compare a discounted Series 11 if those health upgrades are not essential to you.
Who shouldn’t buy one?
Series 10 and 11 owners probably won’t gain enough to justify upgrading, especially because the quoted 24-hour battery life is unchanged. Outdoor adventurers who need satellite connectivity, extended workout tracking or maximum battery life should consider the Ultra 4 instead.
Should I buy an older version of the Apple Watch Series?
A discounted Series 10 or 11 could offer better value if you don’t need the new health sensing or Audio Intelligence features. The Series 9 is also still compatible with watchOS 27. Avoid the Series 8 and older models unless they are exceptionally cheap, because they cannot run watchOS 27 and will miss out on future feature updates.

The Apple Watch Ultra 4 is Apple’s most rugged and capable smartwatch, designed for endurance athletes and outdoor adventurers. It retains the Ultra 3’s 49mm titanium case, 3,000-nit display, Action button, dual-frequency GPS, satellite connectivity, 100-meter water resistance and recreational diving support.
Inside, the new S11 processor powers the redesigned heart-rate sensing system also found in the Series 12. It measures heart rate every five seconds throughout the day and enables Audio Intelligence features including Sound Recognition, Live Rewind and Siri Recap. Live Rewind and Siri Recap are still pending, but are currently being tested in the watchOS 27.3 beta
Key advantages and limitations
Battery life is the Ultra 4’s biggest improvement, increasing from 42 to 50 hours under normal use. Extended Workout mode provides up to 25 hours with full GPS and heart-rate measurements, while Max Extended Workout mode can track outdoor runs and walks for up to 45 hours. Charging is faster too, with a 15-minute charge providing up to 18 hours of use.
Satellite connectivity, precision dual-frequency GPS, diving support and the bright display make it particularly well suited to demanding environments. However, its 49mm case is large and heavy, while charging to 80 percent takes around 45 minutes, compared with approximately 30 minutes for the Series 12. The external design is also largely unchanged. Pricing remains at $799, twice the Series 12’s starting price.
Who should buy the Apple Watch Ultra 4?
Choose the Ultra 4 if you need the longest Apple Watch battery life, highly accurate GPS, satellite connectivity, diving support or extended workout tracking. It is particularly suited to runners, hikers, cyclists, divers and anyone who regularly spends more than a day away from a charger.
Its extended battery life could also appeal to travelers and people working long shifts, even if they don’t participate in extreme sports.
Who shouldn’t buy one?
Most people will be better served by the smaller and less expensive Series 12. It provides the same S11 processor, redesigned heart-rate sensing and principal Audio Intelligence features without the Ultra’s bulk or $799 price. If you don’t need satellite communication, precision GPS, diving support or exceptionally long workout tracking, you are unlikely to benefit from the additional expense.
Should I buy an older Apple Watch Ultra?
The Ultra 3 remains a strong alternative if substantially discounted, although its battery lasts up to 42 rather than 50 hours. The Ultra 2 is the oldest model compatible with watchOS 27 and may also be worth considering at the right price, but it lacks some newer connectivity and battery improvements. Avoid the original Ultra unless it is exceptionally inexpensive, because it cannot run watchOS 27.

The Apple Watch SE 3 is Apple’s most affordable smartwatch and the best-value model in the current lineup. Introduced in September 2025, it brought substantial improvements over the SE 2, including an always-on display, the S10 processor used by the Series 11, temperature sensing, fast charging and 64GB of storage.
It also supports Double Tap and Wrist Flick gestures, on-device Siri and media playback through its speaker. The aluminum case comes in Midnight or Starlight, but there is no longer a Silver option. Prices start at $249/£219, although it has fallen as low as $179 in the Black Friday sale.
Key advantages and limitations
The SE 3 provides the essential Apple Watch experience, including fitness and sleep tracking, Sleep Score, heart-rate alerts, temperature-based cycle tracking, sleep apnea notifications, Fall Detection and Crash Detection. Its Ion-X display glass is four times more crack-resistant than that of the SE 2, while cellular versions add 5G connectivity.
Battery life remains limited to 18 hours, although Low Power Mode extends this to 32 hours. Fast charging reaches approximately 80 percent in 45 minutes, and a 15-minute charge provides around eight hours of use. The SE 3 lacks ECG, Blood Oxygen monitoring, hypertension notifications and the redesigned Health Sensing System found on the Series 12. Its 1,000-nit display, thicker bezels and limited material choices also make it feel less premium.
Who should buy the Apple Watch SE 3?
The SE 3 is ideal for first-time Apple Watch buyers and anyone who wants fitness tracking, notifications and safety features without paying for advanced health sensors. It is also a strong option for children when using the cellular model with Family Setup, and for older users who could benefit from Fall Detection, Emergency SOS and heart-rate monitoring.
Who shouldn’t buy one?
Choose the Series 12 instead if you want ECG, Blood Oxygen monitoring, hypertension notifications, more advanced heart-rate sensing or a brighter, more premium display. Buyers who need multi-day battery life, satellite connectivity or specialist outdoor features should consider the Ultra 4.
Should I buy an older Apple Watch SE?
No. The SE 2 cannot run watchOS 27 and lacks the SE 3’s always-on display, temperature sensing, faster charging, newer gestures and additional storage. Even at a substantial discount, its reduced software lifespan makes it difficult to recommend in 2026.  

							
		


watchOS 27 features: What’s new and what requires Series 12 or Ultra 4
Apple released a new version of the software that runs on the Apple Watch – watchOS 27 – on September 14, 2026, but not every new feature is available on every supported watch. Some improvements are software-led and work across compatible models, while others depend on the S11 chip and redesigned sensors in the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4.
The hardware-dependent health features unique to the 2026 Watches include background heart-rate measurements every five seconds and HRV (heart rate variability) measurements every five minutes. The Series 12 and Ultra 4 also gain the Readiness app, which analyzes recent activity, training load, sleep and health data to produce a daily recovery score. Other exclusives include daytime resting heart-rate and HRV data in Vitals, a real-time chart in the Heart Rate app, more accurate all-day step counting and a Steps complication that updates on the watch face.
The S11 chip also enables Apple’s Audio Intelligence features. Automatic Music Recognition uses Shazam to identify nearby songs and display them in the Smart Stack, while Sound Recognition can detect doorbells, alarms, sirens and crying babies without relying on the iPhone. Live Rewind displays a transcript of the previous 15 seconds of conversation after a double-press of the Digital Crown; it does not save an audio recording. Siri Recap produces high-level summaries of conversations. Live Rewind and Siri Recap are available to test with the watchOS 27.3 and iOS 27.3 betas. These features require an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone 16 or later, excluding iPhone 16e. They initially support English and are not yet available in the EU.
Other watchOS 27 features are more widely available. These include the Dynamic App Grid, redesigned Find My app, menopause and perimenopause tracking, Call Context and Workout Buddy improvements. Apple has also introduced the Longevity section and Health Age.
Compatibility is considerably more restricted than it was with watchOS 26. Series 9 and Ultra 2 are now the oldest supported models, while the SE 3 is the only compatible SE. The Series 6, Series 7, Series 8, SE 2 and original Ultra cannot install watchOS 27. Anyone considering a discounted older Apple Watch should therefore choose a Series 9, Series 10, Series 11, Ultra 2 or Ultra 3 if receiving current feature updates is important. Consider your wrist size and comfort
The watch should feel secure without dominating your wrist or restricting movement. The 40mm SE 3 is the best option for particularly small wrists, while the 42mm Series 12 provides a larger display in a case that remains manageable for most people. If possible, try both sizes in an Apple Store before buying.
Consider display size and readability
A larger screen makes text, notifications and onscreen controls easier to see and use. The 49mm Ultra 4 has the largest display, but its 63g titanium case is substantially heavier than the aluminum Series 12 or SE 3. The 46mm Series 12 offers a spacious display without the Ultra’s additional bulk.
Consider whether you need the Ultra
Don’t choose the Ultra 4 solely because it has the largest screen. Its size makes most sense if you also need its rugged titanium construction, satellite connectivity, precision dual-frequency GPS, diving support or 50-hour battery life. For everyday use, the Series 12 will generally be more comfortable.
Check band compatibility
Apple Watch bands aren’t universally interchangeable. Bands designed for smaller cases generally fit the 38mm, 40mm, 41mm and newer 42mm watches, while larger bands work with 44mm, 45mm, 46mm and 49mm models. However, the older 42mm case belongs to the larger band family, so check the compatibility information before reusing or ordering a band.


						

							


Aluminum, titanium or ceramic: Which Apple Watch material is best?

				
					

				
			
Foundry




Another consideration when buying an Apple Watch is its case material, which affects its durability, weight, appearance and price. Apple currently offers aluminum, titanium and ceramic cases, although the available materials depend on the model.
Aluminum: Best for most people
Aluminum is the lightest and most affordable choice. It is the only material available for the Apple Watch SE 3 and the entry-level option for the Series 12, helping to keep their starting prices at $249 and $399 respectively.
It is a good choice for everyday wear, fitness and sleep tracking because it feels lighter on the wrist than the premium alternatives. The SE 3 uses Ion-X display glass, which Apple says is four times more crack-resistant than that of the SE 2. The aluminum Series 12 has the tougher Ceramic Shield 2 display, which Apple claims is 60 percent more durable than the Ion-X glass used by the aluminum Series 11.
Titanium: Best for premium durability
Titanium is available with the Series 12 and is the only case material offered with the Ultra 4. It provides a more premium finish and is paired with highly scratch-resistant sapphire crystal rather than the glass used on aluminum models.
The Series 12 titanium case is available in Natural or Radiant Gold. It is a good option for anyone who wants a more luxurious and durable everyday watch without moving up to the much larger Ultra.
The Ultra 4 uses a rugged Grade 5 titanium case in Natural or Black. It is designed for outdoor adventures, endurance sports and diving, with a 49mm case, 100-meter water resistance and recreational diving support. However, its size and 63g weight make it less comfortable for smaller wrists and sleep tracking.
Ceramic: Best for distinctive styling
Ceramic returns as a premium Series 12 option in Pearl White and Night Blue. It has a glossy, distinctive finish and uses a sapphire crystal display, but it is heavier and considerably more expensive than the aluminum version. The ceramic cases are also slightly larger than the other Series 12 configurations.
Which material is best for Apple Watch?
For most buyers, aluminum offers the best balance of price, durability and comfort. Choose titanium if you want a more premium finish, sapphire crystal or the Ultra 4’s specialized outdoor capabilities. Ceramic is primarily a style-led luxury choice for buyers who want the most distinctive Series 12 and are prepared to pay more for it.

For most people, the Sport Loop is the best all-round choice because it is light, breathable and easy to adjust. Its softness also makes it particularly comfortable for sleep tracking.
For workouts and swimming, choose a Sport Band or Nike Sport Band. The perforated Nike version provides better ventilation during intense exercise. Divers and regular swimmers should consider the Ocean Band, while runners and hikers may prefer the lighter Trail Loop or more rugged Alpine Loop.
For work or formal occasions, the Milanese Loop, Link Bracelet, Modern Buckle and Magnetic Link provide a smarter appearance. Apple’s Hermès collection offers the most luxurious—and most expensive—options.
Before buying, check that the strap supports your Apple Watch case size and wrist measurement. Solo Loop and Braided Solo Loop straps require particularly careful sizing because they cannot be adjusted with a clasp. Third-party straps can offer excellent value, but quality, fit and fastening security vary considerably.


Do I need a cellular Apple Watch?
Whether you need a cellular Apple Watch depends mainly on how often you plan to leave your iPhone behind. For most buyers, the answer is no: a GPS-only Apple Watch offers better value and can already do a great deal without an active connection to an iPhone.
Away from your iPhone, a GPS Apple Watch can still track workouts, monitor health, record location data, use Apple Pay and play music or podcasts downloaded to the watch. When connected to a known Wi-Fi network, it can also send and receive messages, make calls and use many online services. See our guide to Everything an Apple Watch can do without an iPhone.
Cellular becomes useful when you regularly leave your iPhone at home but still want calls, messages, music streaming, navigation and notifications. This makes it particularly valuable for runners, cyclists, swimmers and gym users who don’t want to carry a phone. It can also provide reassurance when you are walking alone or exercising away from Wi-Fi, because the watch can contact emergency services after a fall or crash using its own mobile connection.
A cellular model is also the right choice when setting up an Apple Watch for a child or older relative who doesn’t have an iPhone. Apple Watch For Your Kids, previously called Family Setup, allows a family member’s watch to be configured from another person’s iPhone. A cellular plan enables calls, messages and location sharing when the watch is away from the managing iPhone.
The drawbacks are cost and redundancy. A cellular Series or SE generally costs more than its GPS equivalent, and you must also pay your network provider a monthly fee. If your iPhone is nearly always in your pocket or bag, the watch will normally use its connection instead, leaving you paying for cellular service that you rarely need. See: I switched to a cellular Apple Watch to prove I didn’t need one.
Our recommendation: The Ultra 4 includes cellular as standard, so there is no GPS-only version. For the Series 12 and SE 3, choose cellular only if you expect to leave your iPhone behind regularly or need Family Setup. Otherwise, save your money and buy the GPS model. For a more detailed comparison, see The pros and cons of a cellular Apple Watch.


						

							


Can you use an Apple Watch without an iPhone?
Yes, but with important caveats. An Apple Watch can do a surprising amount without an iPhone nearby, but an iPhone is required for the initial setup and to manage some settings. You cannot set up an Apple Watch using a Mac, iPad or Android phone.
The exception is Apple Watch For Your Kids, previously called Family Setup. This allows a parent or guardian to use their iPhone to configure a cellular Apple Watch for a child or another family member who doesn’t have an iPhone of their own.
Once it has been set up, an Apple Watch can perform many tasks without its paired iPhone nearby – and some don’t require an internet connection at all. These include:
Tracking workouts and activity: Record runs, walks and other exercises, close Activity rings and collect GPS data. The results sync with the iPhone when it reconnects.
Monitoring health: Measure heart rate, track sleep, log medications and use other health features supported by the particular watch.
Playing downloaded media: Listen to music, podcasts and audiobooks stored on the watch using Bluetooth headphones.
Using Apple Pay: Make contactless payments without an iPhone or internet connection once Apple Pay has been configured.
Using offline tools: Set alarms and timers, use the stopwatch and compass, and view photos that have been synced to the watch.
Other features require either Wi-Fi or a cellular connection when the iPhone isn’t nearby. With an internet connection, the watch can make and receive calls, send messages, check email, stream music and podcasts, use Maps and access online apps and services.
Fall Detection and Crash Detection can recognize an incident without your iPhone nearby, but contacting emergency services requires a suitable connection. Most Apple Watches need cellular coverage or Wi-Fi calling with an internet connection. Apple Watch Ultra 3 and Ultra 4 also support Emergency SOS via satellite in supported countries and regions, including the U.S. and U.K. This allows emergency texting when cellular and Wi-Fi coverage are unavailable, and can relay automatic Fall Detection or Crash Detection alerts if you are unresponsive. Satellite connectivity requires being outdoors with a clear view of the sky and horizon.
An Apple Watch therefore cannot completely replace an iPhone, but it doesn’t need to remain beside it throughout the day. For a complete breakdown, read all the things an Apple Watch can do without an iPhone.


						

							


How we choose the best Apple Watch
Macworld’s Apple Watch recommendations draw on more than a decade of hands-on experience. Our writers have tested and reviewed every generation since the original Apple Watch, comparing each new model with both its current rivals and previous generations before deciding whether it deserves a recommendation.
Our assessment focuses on the factors that make a meaningful difference in everyday use:
Real-world testing: We assess comfort, build quality, display visibility, performance, battery life, charging, health sensors, fitness tracking and software features. We also consider how well the watch performs during everyday activities, workouts and sleep tracking—not simply how its specifications compare on paper.
Value and upgrade potential: A newer or more expensive Apple Watch is not automatically the best choice. We consider whether its improvements justify the price, whether owners of recent models would benefit from upgrading and whether a discounted previous-generation watch offers better value.
Honest recommendations: We clearly identify compromises such as limited battery life, missing health sensors, a bulky design or features that most people are unlikely to use. We don’t recommend a product simply because it has the most impressive specifications.
Advice for different buyers: There is no single Apple Watch that suits everyone. We recommend the Series 12 for most buyers, the SE 3 for those seeking the best value, and the Ultra 4 for endurance athletes and outdoor adventurers who need its longer battery life, rugged construction and specialist capabilities.
Our final recommendations therefore combine extensive testing, expert judgment, price analysis and practical buying advice. The aim is not merely to identify the Apple Watch with the longest feature list, but to help you find the model that provides the right balance of features, comfort and value for the way you will actually use it.


						

							





 FAQ 


1.
Is now a good time to buy an Apple Watch
Now is a good time to buy an Apple Watch because the brand-new Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 went on sale on September 18, 2026. You don’t even have to wait for the Black Friday sales for the best deals, because they are here! See: our Apple Watch Black Friday deals guide and Should I buy an Apple Watch now or wait? 





2.
What is the difference between the Series 12 and SE 3?
The Apple Watch Series 12 offers a brighter, tougher display, premium aluminum, titanium and ceramic cases, and the newer S11 chip. It also includes advanced health features such as ECG, Blood Oxygen monitoring, high-frequency heart-rate sensing and the Readiness app, plus exclusive Audio Intelligence features. Battery life is rated at 24 hours. 
The $249/£219 SE 3 uses the S10 chip, lasts 18 hours and provides essential fitness, sleep and safety features, but lacks the Series 12’s advanced sensors and premium materials.





3.
Can you swim while wearing an Apple Watch?
Yes, you can swim while wearing an Apple Watch, but the level of water resistance varies significantly depending on the model. The Apple Watch Ultra models are the most water-capable in the lineup. They are water-resistant to 100 meters and are suitable for swimming, snorkeling, scuba diving (up to 40 meters), and high-speed water sports. The Ultra models also include a depth gauge (up to 40 meters) and a water temperature sensor, making them a genuine companion for divers and endurance swimmers. 
Apple Watch Series 12, Series 11 and Series 10 are water-resistant to 50 meters and suitable for shallow-water activities such as swimming. They also support snorkeling to 6 meters, but should not be used for scuba diving, waterskiing or other high-velocity water sports. Water resistance can diminish over time.
The Apple Watch SE 3 is also water-resistant to 50 meters and is considered “swimproof”.
Follow these steps to enable Water Lock: 
Before swimming, press the side button to open Control Center. 
Tap the water-drop icon to enable Water Lock. 
After swimming press and hold the Digital Crown to unlock the screen and eject water from the speaker.





4.
Should I buy an old Apple Watch model?
Buying an older Apple Watch can be a great way to save money, but in late 2026, you need to be much more careful than in previous years. The biggest factor is software support, as watchOS 27 dropped support for several relatively recent models.
Apple made a significant change with watchOS 27. The update drops support for the Apple Watch SE 2, Series 6, Series 7, Series 8 and the original Apple Watch Ultra. If you want a watch that will continue to receive the latest features and security updates, you must buy a model with at least an S9 chip. This means the oldest supported models are now the Apple Watch Series 9 and Ultra 2, both from 2023. 
If you are shopping for an older Apple Watch our recommendation is to buy refurbished watches from Apple. Read Should I buy a refurbished Apple Watch? for guidance. Another good option is to look for previous-generation Apple Watch models in major sales events, such as Black Friday. Take a look at the best prices right now in the boxes below.

content:

In a post on Weibo, the blogger known as "Experience More" highlighted the apparently unchanged display cutout in images of the ‌iPhone Air‌ 2 and iPhone 18 dummy models shared by Sonny Dickson last week. The ‌iPhone 18 Pro‌'s revised internal design places the front-facing camera toward the right of the ‌Dynamic Island‌, but adding an Ultra Wide rear camera to the ‌iPhone Air‌ 2 could leave insufficient room for a similar configuration.

Buying refurbished is another smart way to save money, with Apple’s Certified Refurbished Store and reputable retailers offering lower prices while still providing a warranty and years of software support.
In this guide, we’ll explain the best and worst times to buy an iPad, which models are worth buying now, when the next updates are expected, and how to get the best value whether you’re buying new or refurbished. If you’re still deciding which iPad is right for you, see our complete iPad buying guide.

Should you buy an iPad now?
Two iPads are safe to buy without worrying about an imminent replacement: the iPad Air (M4) and iPad Pro (M5). Both were updated recently and aren’t expected to be refreshed until 2027.
The entry-level iPad (A16) and iPad mini (A17 Pro) are a different story. Both are widely expected to receive updates before the end of 2026, making them harder to recommend unless you find them at a significant discount.

The iPad Pro (M5), launched in October 2025, remains Apple’s most capable tablet. It combines the M5 chip with a stunning Tandem OLED ProMotion display, support for up to 2TB of storage, and class-leading performance. The next update isn’t expected until 2027.
That said, it’s the right choice only if you’ll benefit from its extra power. Creative professionals working with demanding apps, large media projects, or intensive multitasking will appreciate what it offers. Most other buyers will find the iPad Air delivers a very similar everyday experience for considerably less money. Likewise, children and casual users are generally better served by the standard iPad or iPad mini than by Apple’s most expensive tablet.

							
		


When is the best time to buy an iPad

				
					

				
			
Foundry




The best time to buy an iPad is during major shopping events, particularly Black Friday and Amazon Prime Day, when retailers such as Amazon, Best Buy, and Walmart typically offer their biggest discounts.
Black Friday and Cyber Monday (November/December)
Black Friday is usually the best time of the year to buy an iPad. In 2025, every current iPad model reached its lowest-ever price during the Black Friday sales, with discounts of up to $150. In 2026, we’ve seen some great savings, including the iPad mini at $599, the A16 iPad at $379, and the M4 iPad Air from $649/£669. See Black Friday iPad deals.
Amazon Prime Day (June/July and October)
Amazon now holds two major Prime Day sales each year – one in June or July and another in October – and both regularly feature excellent iPad deals.
The June 2026 event was particularly significant because in the middle of the sale Apple increased iPad prices by $100 to $300, which made the discounts even larger.
The October Prime Day sale often matches or comes close to Black Friday discounts and is another excellent time to buy. See Prime Day iPad deals.
During Apple’s Back to School promotion
If you’re a student, teacher, or work in education, Apple’s Education Store offers year-round discounts on most iPads. During Apple’s annual Back to School promotion in the summer, eligible buyers also receive a free gift card, making it one of the best times to buy directly from Apple.
Note that the criteria are very strict for shopping in Apple’s Education Store. Customers need to verify their eligibility through UNiDAYS before accessing Education Store pricing.


						

							


When shouldn’t you buy an iPad?
The worst time to buy an iPad is just before Apple releases a new model. You’ll often end up paying full price for a device that’s about to be replaced, while retailers discount the outgoing model to clear stock.
There are a few other situations where it’s worth thinking twice before buying:
If a major sale is just around the corner: If Amazon Prime Day or Black Friday is only a few weeks away, it’s usually worth waiting. These sales consistently offer the biggest iPad discounts of the year, often saving you $100 or more compared with buying at full price.
If you want a laptop replacement: An iPad can replace a laptop for some people, but it becomes much less compelling once you add accessories. A Magic Keyboard or similar case can add hundreds of dollars to the cost, bringing the total close to – or even above – the price of a MacBook. With the arrival of the $699 MacBook Neo, the value equation has shifted further. A similarly equipped iPad and keyboard can cost more while still being limited to iPadOS and mobile apps rather than full desktop software.
If you’re buying an older iPad: Discounts on older or refurbished iPads can be tempting, but always check how long they’ll continue to receive software updates. iPadOS 27 dropped support for several older models, including the 2018 iPad Pro (3rd generation), 2019 iPad mini (5th generation) and 2020 iPad (8th generation). Buying an unsupported model means you’ll miss future features, security updates and, eventually, app compatibility.
If you want Apple Intelligence: Apple Intelligence isn’t available on every iPad. It requires an M1 chip or later (iPad Air and iPad Pro) or the A17 Pro or A20 Pro chip in the iPad mini. The entry-level iPad (A16) does not support Apple’s AI features, making it a less future-proof purchase.
If you don’t need cellular:  Think carefully before paying extra for a 5G cellular model. Cellular connectivity typically adds more than $100 to the purchase price, and you’ll usually need a separate data plan. If you already carry an iPhone, using Personal Hotspot is often a far cheaper alternative.
If fast wired transfers matter: Most people won’t notice USB speeds, but they matter if you regularly transfer large files via cable. The standard iPad is limited to USB 2.0 (480Mbps), the iPad mini supports 5Gbps, the iPad Air 10Gbps, while the iPad Pro offers Thunderbolt speeds of up to 40Gbps. 


						

							


What is the best iPad price right now?
Apple rarely discounts iPads. In fact, in June 2026, Apple increased iPad prices by $100 to $200, citing unprecedented component cost increases. The price rise came in the middle of Amazon’s Prime Day sale, during which we saw record-low prices. Prices that low are unlikely to return until a major sales event such as October Prime Day or Black Friday.

Other ways to save money when buying an iPad
If you’re flexible about where and when you buy, there are several ways to reduce the cost of a new iPad.
Buy a refurbished iPad: Apple’s Certified Refurbished Store is one of the best places to save money. Refurbished iPads undergo Apple’s full testing process, receive a new battery and outer shell where required, include the same one-year warranty as a new device, and are eligible for AppleCare+. Prices are typically around 15% lower than buying new, with savings of up to $450 on some iPad Pro models.
Use Apple’s Education Store: Students, teachers, and education staff can save 5–15% through Apple’s Education Store all year round. During Apple’s annual Back to School promotion, qualifying purchases also include a free gift, such as AirPods or an Apple Pencil. In the U.S., eligibility now needs to be verified through UNiDAYS before accessing Education Store pricing. Read: How to shop at Apple’s Education Store.
Trade in your old iPad: Apple’s Trade In programme can significantly reduce the cost of a new iPad. For the highest trade-in value, upgrade before Apple announces a replacement model, as trade-in prices typically fall once new devices are released.
Shop during major sales: The biggest discounts usually come from retailers such as Amazon, Best Buy, and Walmart during Prime Day and Black Friday. Apple itself rarely discounts iPads, instead offering gift cards during promotions such as Black Friday and Back to School. While those offers can be worthwhile, third-party retailers almost always provide larger cash discounts.


						

							


Is buying a refurbished iPad a good idea?

				
					

				
			
Apple




Buying a refurbished iPad is one of the best ways to save money. You can often afford a model with more storage or even an iPad Pro for the price of a new entry-level iPad.
The key is to buy refurbished, not simply used. A properly refurbished iPad has been tested, repaired if necessary, and checked to ensure it works like new. A used iPad sold privately is typically sold “as is”, with no warranty, and could even be locked to the previous owner’s Apple ID.
Buy from Apple’s Certified Refurbished Store
The safest option is Apple’s Certified Refurbished Store. Every refurbished iPad is fully tested, fitted with a new battery and outer shell where required, cleaned, and repackaged with all original accessories. You also receive:
A one-year warranty, just like a new iPad.
The option to purchase AppleCare+.
Original accessories and packaging.
Prices are typically around 15% lower than buying new.
What to look for
If you’re buying from a third-party retailer, pay attention to a few key details:
Software support: Choose a model that will continue receiving iPadOS updates for several years. Older devices, such as the 2018 iPad Pro (3rd generation) and 2020 iPad (8th generation), no longer support iPadOS 27.
Storage: Aim for at least 128GB. Older 32GB and 64GB models can quickly run out of space with modern apps and games.
Condition: Check the retailer’s grading system so you know what cosmetic wear to expect.
Warranty: Buy from a seller that includes a warranty—ideally for at least one year.
Where to buy 
Apple Certified Refurbished: The safest choice, with the same warranty and support as a new iPad.
Reputable refurbishers: Retailers such as Back Market, Best Buy, and Amazon Renewed often offer deeper discounts, but always check the condition grading and warranty before buying.
If you buy from a trusted retailer and choose a model that still has years of software support ahead of it, a refurbished iPad can offer excellent value while saving you a significant amount of money.


						

							


Do you need to upgrade your current iPad?
Whether it’s time to replace your iPad depends on four things: software support, performance, battery life, and whether you’re missing features you actually want.
Your iPad no longer receives updates
The most important reason to upgrade is when your iPad stops receiving software and security updates. Apple typically provides major iPadOS updates for around six to eight years, with security updates often continuing for a while afterwards. See: How long does Apple support iPads?
As long as your iPad still receives security updates, it’s generally safe to keep using. Once those updates end, however, you’ll eventually lose app compatibility and expose yourself to increasing security risks.
As of 2026, iPads with an A14 chip or newer, or any M-series iPad, support iPadOS 27. Older models, including the 2018 iPad Pro and 2019 iPad Air, have reached the end of major software support.
It feels slow or the battery no longer lasts
Performance and battery life naturally decline with age. If apps take a long time to open, crash frequently, or the interface feels sluggish even after restarting, your iPad may be struggling to keep up. 
Which are the best retailers to buy an iPad from?
Aside from Apple (View the iPad in the Apple Store and View the iPad in the Apple Store U.K). There are a number of third-party resellers that frequently discount the different iPad models.

Similarly, if the battery no longer lasts through a typical day or the iPad shuts down unexpectedly, it may be time to replace the device – or at least the battery.
You want Apple Intelligence
One of the biggest reasons to upgrade today is Apple Intelligence. Apple’s AI features require an M-series chip or an A17 Pro processor.
If you own the current entry-level iPad (A16) or an older model, you won’t be able to use features such as Writing Tools, Priority Notifications, or Clean Up in Photos.
When you probably don’t need to upgrade
If your iPad still runs the latest version of iPadOS, performs well, and meets your needs, there’s little reason to replace it.
Owners of the M1 iPad Air or newer, as well as recent iPad Pro models, are unlikely to notice a dramatic difference in everyday tasks by upgrading to the latest generation. Unless you need a specific new feature or substantially more performance, you’re usually better off keeping your current iPad for another year or two.

title: iPhone Sales Ban in India Sought by Startup Over NameDrop Feature
content:
Apple will have to contend with a patent lawsuit in India over its NameDrop contact-sharing feature, as a U.S. startup is seeking 15 billion rupees (approximately $162 million) in damages and restrictions on sales of devices that include the feature, reports TechCrunch.


The company behind the lawsuit is GG Technologies, which is responsible for the contact-sharing app StayTouch. It filed the case in the Bombay High Court in October. According to court documents seen by TechCrunch, the company alleges NameDrop infringes its Indian patent covering technology that allows nearby phones to exchange contact details without manual pairing.

The startup is asking the court to prevent Apple from selling or importing iPhones and Apple Watches that support the NameDrop feature in India. The case had not yet been listed for a hearing. 

GG Technologies launched StayTouch in 2019, and received its Indian patent in July 2024 after applying in 2021. The lawsuit apparently followed unsuccessful mediation between the companies, according to the startup, which also sued Apple in the U.S. in April over related patent infringement claims.

In August, the International Trade Commission (ITC) opened an investigation in the U.S. into Apple's alleged patent infringement, following the complaint from GG Technologies. The startup wants to see an order that could block imports of infringing Apple devices into the country, as well as restrictions on their sale.

NameDrop back in June 2023 with the release of iOS 17. The feature lets users exchange contact information by bringing compatible devices close together, although sharing requires user confirmation. It can be easy to forget that the feature exists, and it's not really clear how many people use it on a regular basis.

title: Apple is taking big swings again. So what if it misses a few?
content:
Macworld





John Ternus could be forgiven for having second thoughts about this whole CEO thing. It all seemed so simple a few months ago: a typically unselfish Tim Cook had saved up multiple groundbreaking products so his successor could unveil them in the first few months of his tenure and hit the ground running. But it turns out that innovation is a double-edged sword, not an easy win.
The iPhone Duo, Apple’s first ever folding phone, should have been a celebration of the company’s best qualities. A classic example of Apple’s patient perfectionism, the device was as thoughtfully designed as it was late to market. Arriving just as foldables threatened to break into the mainstream (it will accelerate this process by its very existence, of course), the Duo corrected many common issues: its stubbier form factor means the internal screen is rectangular, not square; the clever hinge design looks superb and feels reassuringly robust; and that matte-finish inner screen delivers one of the least obtrusive creases on the market right now.
But then disaster struck. A number of units proved seriously defective, failing to open or close properly, making strange noises, or displaying unwanted lines on the screen. So much for that robust hinge. It was probably a bad batch rather than a fundamental issue with the design, but enough customers were affected for Apple to be moved to make a public statement and publish a troubleshooting guide. And then, to add insult to injury, some affected users (who’d each paid out at least $1,999) had to wait for replacements because of supply shortages.
Of course, the Duo’s problems can’t entirely be blamed on its innovative design. The 18 Pro, which was launched at the same time, offers largely the same design and feature set as its predecessor but suffered issues of its own, including crackling speakers, random reboots, and an inability to place emergency calls. But in most cases these were bugs which could be quickly fixed via software, not device-breaking faults. They certainly garnered less media coverage than Hingegate, and most observers would regard the 18 Pro as more of a success than the Duo, at least in the short term.
The Duo, then, was not the straightforward slam dunk John Ternus must have hoped for, nor did it start his reign with an easy win. It was a complicated and problematic launch: interesting, risky, flawed. Apple, however, kept on going. October brought the announcement of two more groundbreaking Apple launches in the form of its first ever touchscreen laptop and its first smart home hub. However, neither proved to be the simple success which any newbie CEO longs for.
Most reviewers, I will grant you, love the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display. (My colleague Roman Loyola says it “raises the bar of Apple excellence.”) But the positive notes have a curious equivocation about the marquee feature. The display is amazing, but why did Apple feel the give it a touchscreen, with all of the corresponding price and design compromises? “It’s not a spotlight feature,” says Roman. “Touch isn’t even in the name of this new MacBook. I’d go so far as to say that the laptop just happens to have Touch. Apple hasn’t done anything here that requires Touch, so you can buy it, never use Touch, and you won’t miss out on anything.”
So, the single thing that’s truly new is almost tangential to the laptop’s usefulness. Which even in a five-star review must be an oddly disappointing response to one of Apple’s most radical Mac launches in years.
Still, it could have been a lot worse, and in fact, it soon would be. The HomeView home hub is yet another entirely new venture for the company, which means both excitement and risk. And the risk part of the equation came to the forefront as hundreds of buyers complained about dozens of separate software issues with their brand-new devices. One commenter called it the “worst Apple launch ever” (do the words “hockey-puck mouse” mean nothing to you?) and the atmosphere could only be described as mutinous.
My suspicion, after conferring with another colleague who’s been testing out a unit and then asking Apple’s product managers for their thoughts, is that HomeView will turn out to be more 18 Pro than Duo. Even the “worst launch ever” commenter conceded that the HomeView’s hardware is strong; it just has lots of bugs. Or perhaps I should say had lots of bugs, because that same colleague found that updating the device’s software delivered a much smoother experience than was reported elsewhere, and Apple has since mobilized to roll out further patches. Not everything will work perfectly, as is always the case with new products, but software tends to be a lot easier to fix than hardware.
So it’s been a mixed bag of a tenure so far for John Ternus. He’s had the privilege of unveiling three of the most momentous Apple products of the decade, and the burden of responding to those products’ inevitable teething troubles.
First, novelty means unfamiliarity: I’ve been using the iPhone Duo for several weeks and still find the physical design awkward and the software interface confusing. It will take time to get used to both of those factors, just as it will take time to grow accustomed to using touch on a laptop, or to find space in our lives for a home hub with a screen. It’s easier to understand the purpose of a product if you’ve already used one that’s essentially the same.
Second, entirely new products are difficult to develop because so much needs to be designed from scratch. The iPhone Duo’s hinge is a miracle of modern engineering, but that doesn’t make it immune to manufacturing errors; rather, because it’s so new and so innovative, they become almost inevitable. The HomeView software platform is also completely new, which means more to test and more scope to miss bugs. The tech industry worships the new, but new things break. It’s part of the deal.
There have been ups and downs, but I’ve enjoyed Apple’s bold new approach this fall. With the Duo, the company dared to try something new after umpteen near-identical iPhone updates; with the touchscreen MacBook and HomeView it showed a willingness to radically evolve a successful existing product and to move into an entirely new market. The company took risks, and was punished as much as it was rewarded.
Looking at this fall’s complaints and controversies, it’s easy to see why massive corporations are tempted to play it safe most of the time. And why, in the past, Apple has so often favored cautious iteration. Releasing a mildly tweaked version of a product which was already successful is, ironically, exactly the sort of easy win which John Ternus must have craved. Actual innovation is a nightmare that goes wrong as often as it goes right. And when it fails, an innovative product fails in public.
But as risky and occasionally embarrassing as it can be, innovation is still the way forward. I’m sure that in time Apple’s turn towards radical innovation this year will prove to be not just the correct but the necessary decision. You can’t make the same product forever. It just might have been kinder to take at least some of the risks before the new guy took over.

USB-C and its Thunderbolt variant are the most up-to-date standards of the USB connector. They allow data-transfer speeds of up to 80Gbps, can fast-charge devices up to 240W, and conveniently fit in a port either way up—which means that you can wave bye-bye to the age-old USB guessing game of “Which way does it go in?”.
USB-C is no one-trick pony—handling data transfer, video output and power input. You’ll find faster variants of USB-C (called Thunderbolt 3, 4 or 5) on Macs. Each version of Thunderbolt is backwards compatible with USB-C so the adapters reviewed here will all work with modern Macs—from the MacBooks Neo, Air and Pro, through to the desktop iMac, Mac mini and Studio. USB-C’s 5-10Gbps speeds will limit some of Thunderbolt’s more impressive 40 to 80Gbps potential but for most people even 5Gbps is fast enough. If super-fast data transfer is one of your requirements, a number of hubs reviewed below do use Thunderbolt or 40Gbps USB4. Find out more in our Thunderbolt 5 vs Thunderbolt 4 vs Thunderbolt 3 comparison and also our chart at the end showing all the ports of Apple’s recent Macs.

				
					

				
			
Apple




In general, an “adapter” works with a single port (such as USB-A or Ethernet) while a “hub” gives you multiple ports. If you require even more, then look for a “docking station” or “dock“. Docks usually come with their own power supply, while hubs require a separate USB-C charger if you need a power source. If you’re after a full desktop setup for your MacBook, look out for our recommendations for the best USB-C and Thunderbolt docking stations for MacBooks.
Apple sells its own range of USB-C adapters to HDMI, VGA and more, but they are overpriced and underpowered compared to the premium USB-C hubs and adapters we have reviewed here. We haven’t included the many much cheaper but lower-quality versions you can find online as we recommend only from trusted and tested makers. There are plenty of affordable solutions tested and reviewed here that are of a higher quality.
Look for each hub’s video capability for connecting to external displays. Most support only one monitor, but some offer two—note that more than two usually requires an extra software install.
Passthrough power will likely also be of interest to MacBook users. 60W Power Delivery (PD) will work even for the 16-inch MacBook Pro (just), but more watts equals a faster charge.
Note that the ports on the MacBook Neo are USB-C and only one of them is properly data-ready at 10Gbps, with the other just for charging. Read more on how the MacBook Neo’s USB-C ports are different. As it has just one data port, a USB-C hub becomes a must for expanding the Neo’s potential—read our roundup of the best MacBook Neo accessories.

This adapter is designed to help owners of really quite old Macs smoothly transition to using USB-C. You may well have devices such as hard drives and external displays that use Thunderbolt 2 connections. This little gadget lets you keep using them with your MacBook or new MacBook Pro.
It also allows new Thunderbolt 3, 4 and 5 devices to connect to a Mac with Thunderbolt 2 ports–but to take advantage of it this way round Apple advises you need to be running macOS Sierra or above.

							
		
Which extra ports do you need in a hub
Many MacBook users connect their laptop to one or more external displays for greater screen space. You can connect to monitors using USB-C (via adapters to non-USB-C monitors) or better a dedicated video port, such as HDMI or DisplayPort. Check the hub specs to see which displays they support: some are limited to HD displays, others support 4K (also known as UHD) displays. The refresh rate is also important. 4K at 30Hz is fine for most productivity and browsing tasks, but watching video or playing games demands higher refresh rates of at least 60Hz.
You may need some legacy non-reversible USB-A ports, and most adapters and hubs have at least one for your non-USB-C memory sticks and drives. Look for at least USB 3.0, which has a speedy bandwidth of 5Gbps compared to the lamentably sluggish USB 2.0’s 480Mbps.
To fast-charge an iPhone, you need a minimum of 18W and it has to be USB-C, so look for extra USB-C slots with charging power, which are more capable than USB-A.
Other ports to look for in a hub include Ethernet for faster wired Internet access (without the flakiness of Wi-Fi). You can choose from standard Gigabit Ethernet (1000Mbps) or 2.5Gb and even 5Gb and 10Gb Ethernet (2500-10000Mbps), although the faster Ethernet requires the whole network to support that speed.
An SD or microSD card reader is perfect for adding inexpensive portable storage to your system. Card readers come at different speeds: UHS-I at 104MBps, and UHS-II at 312MBps; although some are slower at 60MBps.
Look for hubs that offer passthrough charging, so you can charge your laptop even though you are using up one of the laptop’s USB-C ports for the hub itself. Most don’t ship with a charger, so you’ll need to add your own, and remember that it needs to be a 100W charger to give 85W and above charging if offered by the hub. Lower wattage chargers are fine but will limit the hub’s charging potential. Couple your hub with one of the best Mac USB-C chargers. See how much power your MacBook needs in our advice below the list of recommended hubs and adapters.
You can also buy USB-C adapters for the many older display standards out there, such as VGA and DVI. We’ve picked the best for you below.
Many hubs and docks aren’t compatible with Apple’s SuperDrive CD/DVD drive. We’ve found few dock makers that offers compatibility with the SuperDrive, the Caldigit Thunderbolt Element Hub and OWC Thunderbolt Dock being two that do.
Which ports does each Mac have?
Here are the onboard ports on all of Apple’s current and recent Macs:
MacBook Neo: 2x USB-C (one for 10Gbps data and one for charging), 3.5mm headphone jack
MacBook Air: 2x Thunderbolt 4, MagSafe 3 charging port, 3.5mm headphone jack
MacBook Pro (plain M4/M5/M6): 3x Thunderbolt 4, MagSafe 3 charging port, HDMI, SDXC Card Reader (250MBps), 3.5mm headphone jack
MacBook Pro (M4/M5 Pro/Max): 3x Thunderbolt 5, MagSafe 3 charging port, HDMI, SDXC Card Reader (250MBps), 3.5mm headphone jack
iMac (24-inch): 2x Thunderbolt 4/USB4 or 4x Thunderbolt 4, 3.5mm headphone jack, optional Gigabit Ethernet
Mac mini M4/M6: 3x Thunderbolt 4, 2x USB-C (10Gbps), HDMI, Gigabit Ethernet, 3.5mm headphone jack
Mac mini M4 Pro: 3x Thunderbolt 5, 2x USB-C (10Gbps), HDMI, Gigabit Ethernet, 3.5mm headphone jack
Mac mini M5 Pro: 3x Thunderbolt 5, 2x USB-C (10Gbps), HDMI, 2.5Gb Ethernet, 3.5mm headphone jack
Mac Studio M4 Pro, M5 Max: 4x Thunderbolt 5, 2x USB-C (10Gbps), 2x USB-A (5Gbps), HDMI, 10Gb Ethernet, SDXC Card Reader (312MBps), 3.5mm headphone jack
Mac Studio M3/M5 Ultra: 6x Thunderbolt 5, 2x USB-A (5Gbps), HDMI, 10Gb Ethernet, SDXC Card Reader (312MBps), 3.5mm headphone jack
Mirrored or Extended Modes for Mac displays
When you attach more than one external display to a Mac you can choose between various setups. Most hubs with more than one video port—usually HDMI—can mirror your MacBook’s screen, but most can at best handle showing a different screen to the Mac but not different to each other when attempting Extended Mode.
For full extended Mode, where each of the screens shows a different image and you treat each as an extension to your workspace—moving your cursor and windows easily between the displays—you will likely need a hub or dock that supports free third-party DisplayLink software, which is easy to download and install. Included above are reviews of the Plugable Dual and Quad HDMI adapters, both of which work with DisplayLink. DisplayLink enables multiple screens even with plain M1 and M2 MacBooks that are technically limited to just one external display.
If you need even more ports than you’ll find on a hub, check our reviews of the best DisplayLink docks.

				
					

				
			
Baseus




How much power does each MacBook require for smooth running
Check the Power Delivery (PD) charging power each hub or adapter offers connected laptops or iPads. 
The MacBook Neo charges at 20W.
The 13-inch MacBook Air charges at 30W, but can fast-charge at 70W and above.
The 13-inch MacBook Pro and 15-inch MacBook Air charge at 70W for fast charging, but even 45W would keep you topped up if running basic tasks at the time. Apple recommends at least 60W for the 14-inch M6 MacBook Pro.
The higher-end 14-inch (M3/M4/M5/M6, M4/M5 Pro/Max) and 16-inch MacBook Pro require at least 96W for fast charging, but can cope at 60W or 70W. The 16-inch MacBook Pro prefers 140W, but is fine with 94W unless under extreme processing tasks.
You can certainly use a charger at lower power, but remember that it will power up slower than when using a higher-wattage charger, and if too low your laptop might run out of juice altogether when maxed out on power-hungry apps and devices. And you can use a higher-power charger without any concerns. The device being charged decides how much power it requires.

title: Gurman: Siri Layoffs Spared Newer AI Systems, But Problems Persist
content:
Apple's recent Siri layoffs affected employees working on the assistant's older infrastructure rather than its newer AI systems, according to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman.


In his latest "Power On" newsletter, Gurman said employees have yet to notice a major difference in how Apple operates despite efforts to accelerate development and spread significant releases throughout the year. He added that the company faces growing competition from AI developers that update their models and services far more frequently than Apple's annual operating system cycle.

Within software engineering chief Craig Federighi's organization, Apple apparently follows an internal release calendar labeled A through G, with engineering work tied to specific software versions and launch windows. Depending on the release, the roadmap and features for a major operating system update are largely determined by late summer or early fall of the preceding year.

Gurman argued that this structure leaves Apple with limited flexibility to respond to competitors' breakthroughs during the subsequent development cycle. Gurman also criticized ‌Siri‌'s slow responses, limited third-party integration, and seemingly worsening dictation.

more advanced AI agent, but Gurman does not expect it to arrive before late 2027. He warned that rival agents could become difficult to abandon as they accumulate users' preferences and connected accounts, although Apple's reputation for privacy and deeper platform access could help it compete. ‌Siri‌'s multistep control of Apple apps is expected to launch in December, with third-party app support following in 2027.

title: Apple Reportedly Plans to Release These Products in February or March
content:
Apple plans to unveil an iPhone 18e, iPhone 18, updated entry-level iPad, and new MacBook Neo and MacBook Air models around February or March next year, according to the latest word from Bloomberg's Mark Gurman.


In his Power On newsletter today, Gurman said Apple has some additional products planned for the first half of 2027, including the iPhone Air 2 and new iPad Air and iPad Pro models, but he said those devices will likely be unveiled as part of a second launch a "little bit" later. So, perhaps we will see those products unveiled later in March or in April.


iPhone 18e: A20 chip, 9GB of RAM, and longer battery life.

iPhone 18: A20 chip, 9GB of RAM, and longer battery life.

iPad: A19 chip with Apple Intelligence support, N1 chip with Wi-Fi 7 support, and Apple's power-efficient C1X modem in cellular models.

MacBook Neo: A19 Pro chip, 12GB of RAM, and potentially new color options.

MacBook Air: M6 chip.

iPhone Air 2: A20 Pro chip, Ultra Wide camera, a smaller Dynamic Island, longer battery life, and Apple's C2 modem with mmWave support in the U.S. and "meaningfully faster" upload speeds compared to the current model's C1X modem.

iPad Air: M5 chip, OLED display, thinner and lighter design, and potentially the Acoustic Display feature that debuted on the iPad mini.

iPad Pro: M6 chip or M7 chip and a vapor chamber cooling system.

title: New MacBook Neo now expected in spring 2027
content:
It's always been clear that a MacBook Neo refresh is coming. A new report slightly refines the timetable for the new model, and new colors may arrive with that update too.


MacBook Neo is already the Mac laptop for most people
Among the multiple previous reports of Apple planning a second-generation MacBook Neo, Bloomberg said that one would be released in the first half of 2027. Now the same publication is back to narrow that down further to spring.
Specifically, the new claim is that this second MacBook New is codenamed J701, and that Apple will release subsequent generations annually. It's said that it is to match the release cycle of the MacBook Pro and the MacBook Air, and that Apple is aiming it at the Chromebook and lower-cost Windows PC market.
